en: In the seventh fascicle,

Master Ji establishes the distinctions between the three stages based on whether they are associated with or free from vitarka and vicāra and their defilement or freedom from defilement; he does not base them on their seeds.
Regarding the presence or absence of manifestation,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya* offers three brief interpretations. According to one interpretation:
The third stage is established based on the correspondence between two preceding and succeeding moments.
This refers to the coarse mind and mental factors of the desire realm and the first dhyāna,
because they can exist in a continuous succession where vitarka and vicāra are mutually associated.
This is called the stage with vitarka and vicāra.
In the intermediate dhyāna, the coarse mind and mental factors that previously existed in succession are definitively absent from vitarka.
Because it can only be associated with vicāra,
it is called the stage of "without vitarka and with vicāra.
This refers to all minds and mental factors of the stages from the second dhyāna upward.

That which is a continuous succession of preceding and succeeding moments and is definitely not associated with vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) is called the stage without vitarka and without vicāra.
This applies to the stage of the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the intermediate dhyāna, wherein subtle mind and mental factors are not associated with vitarka and vicāra.
Furthermore, all forms, dissociated formations, and all unconditioned phenomena are also said to be stages without vitarka and without vicāra,
because they do not associate with vitarka and vicāra.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:
"The stages with vitarka and vicāra, and the stage with no vitarka but only vicāra, are invariably stages possessed of mind.

[Excluded are] the mindless states of sleep, the mindless state of fainting, the attainment of non-ideation, birth in the realm of non-ideation, the attainment of cessation, and the realm of nirvana without remainder."
These are also called the "mindless stages. According to one interpretation, these three are established based on the distinction between two types of detachment from desire:
namely, the dharmas of the desire realm and those of the first dhyāna, which are considered provisional designations.
That which has not yet abandoned desire for both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) is called the stage with vitarka and vicāra.
As for the provisional designation of the various dharmas in the intermediate dhyāna:
When vitarka has already been abandoned but vicāra has not yet been abandoned,
it is called the stage of "without vitarka and with only vicāra."
Regarding all phenomena in the stages from the second dhyāna upward,
those who are designations (prajñapti) have already become free from both vitarka and vicāra;
these are called the stages without vitarka and without vicāra.
If one has already become free from desire regarding the lower stages,
that stage may also be called "without vitarka and without vicāra. Therefore,
the fourth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
In this context, it is called the stage free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*) because of the abandonment of the desire for applied and sustained thought,
not because they do not manifest.
Why is this? Because for one who has not yet abandoned the desires of the desire realm,
it is due to the distinction of the mental attention (*manasikāra*) involved in instruction.
At one time, there is also the manifestation of mental activity without vitarka and without vicāra;
for one who has already abandoned desire for vitarka and vicāra,
there is also the manifestation of vitarka and vicāra.
Regarding the meaning of "as when emerging from that meditative absorption and being born in that stage":
in terms of the actual reality, these three are established solely with respect to realms and stages.
That is to say, they refer to all contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena within the realm of desire and the first dhyāna.
Because both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are present therein, it is called the First Ground.
Because the contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas of the intermediate dhyāna contain no vitarka and possess only vicāra, it is called the Second Ground.
Because all contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena in the stages from the second dhyāna upward are devoid of both vitarka and vicāra, it is called the third stage. Thus,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle four, states:
In this context, the desire realm and the first dhyāna— whether as meditative absorption or as a birth-state—
are called the stage with vitarka and vicāra. The intermediate dhyāna—
whether as meditative absorption or as a birth-state— is [the stage without vitarka and with only vicāra].
The stage called "without vitarka and with only vicāra" consists of the second dhyāna and above,
including the entirety of the form realm (rūpadhātu) and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
The stage called "without vitarka and without vicāra" consists of these same levels.
The untainted, conditioned concentration of the first dhyāna is also called the stage with vitarka and vicāra;
for one enters this concentration by taking suchness as its object, based upon the factors of vitarka and vicāra.
Because it does not proceed by way of the manifestation of conceptual discrimination.
The rest is as previously stated. If the three stages were established based on association and based on the departure from desire, they would not encompass all phenomena exhaustively.
It is also greatly confused;
although it is said that stages such as those with vitarka and vicāra possess only mind.
This explains the stages (*bhūmi*) according to the coarse characteristics of a single door. Within this door,
it speaks only of the stages from the second dhyāna upward, which are free from both vitarka and vicāra.

The state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), birth among the non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), and the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) are termed the "mindless ground" (*acittikā bhūmi*).
All other states are termed the "ground with mind" (*sacittikā bhūmi*).
Following this, there are four gates for establishing their similarities and differences.
As will be explained later: although it is said here that because of the absence of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*),
these are called the stages "without applied and sustained thought," this refers only to the stages from the second *dhyāna* upward.
This is because they have necessarily already abandoned desire for applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).

It is not said that the various factors of the lower stages which have already abandoned desire for applied and sustained thought may also be called "without applied or sustained thought" (*avitarkāvicāra*).
If this were the case,
then even those dharmas of the higher stages that have not yet abandoned the vitarka and vicāra of the lower stages would also have to be described as "with vitarka and vicāra," and so forth.
Establishing it in this way would result in great confusion.
Therefore, these three are established solely in relation to the upper and lower realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*). Now, considering this intent:
the states "with vitarka and vicāra" and "without vitarka and with only vicāra" are not explained based on whether they are defiled or free from defilement.
However, if this treatise merely explains the stage that is without vitarka and without vicāra, it would not be exhaustive of the principle. How, then,
can it be said that the distinction between the three stages is established based on being with or without defilement?
If one is in a lower realm and achieves the defilements of the third dhyāna stage, it should be called the "third stage";
however, since it has already been abandoned according to what has been detached from, it should not belong to that stage. Now, one must question this interpretation of the third master.

By what means are the distinctions between realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*) established? They are established by the differences in coarseness and subtlety among the factors belonging to those stages. How are those differences in coarseness and subtlety established? They must necessarily depend on the distinctions among the factors bound by defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
The untainted factors that are free from defilement and depend upon this stage are also distinct.
Since those already abandoned belong to the category of factors with outflows belonging to this stage,
they are subsumed under that stage.
Regarding the statement "possessing defilement":
because there is active manifestation of defilement,
although the body exists in a lower realm and thus possesses the seeds of the three realms, it is not designated as belonging to those three stages.
As for the term "detached from defilement," it refers to the sense of being born in a higher stage; thus,
it does not pertain to the preceding stage.
It does not state that being free from this defilement means one is no longer in this stage;
thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* text is correct and differs from the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* treats this solely on the basis of the second dhyāna and above,
as previously discussed in the third master’s interpretation. Furthermore,
it is explained that the term "possessing defilement" (*saraṇa*) used here [refers to this].
There is the manifestation of those defilements;
that which is free from defilement is the untainted (anāsrava) and so forth.
According to the stage from which one is free of defilement—that is, because the previously defiled stage is now abandoned—it is called "freedom from defilement.
Accordingly, there is a distinction between these two types of existence: that with defilement and freedom from defilement.
The dharmas of the various stages differ;
all that is appropriate to each stage is subsumed under those two types [of defilement and purification].
It is not said that there is defilement belonging to that specific stage.
Since it would be otherwise if one were free from defilement,
there is no contradiction in the text;
this differs from the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Since the *Yogācārabhūmi* speaks only of the third stage (*bhūmi*),
this true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) likewise belongs to that third stage.
It takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object by relying on the states of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Because one has entered this meditative absorption,
it does not manifest through the activity of conceptual discrimination;
for all untainted phenomena, being by nature free from defilement, depend upon those other factors.
It is still that very stage; how much more so for one who has already abandoned defilement?
The contaminated dharmas of the three stages do not belong to those three stages.
Therefore, the text is correct in its meaning;
otherwise, it would constitute an incorrect interpretation. As it says in [the *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*], fascicle 56:

Question: If one is born in the second dhyāna or in a higher stage, and visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so forth, which are accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, are present before one, how can this stage be said to be without vitarka and vicāra?
If they are not present before one, how can one perceive the objects of those stages through the material sense faculties belonging to them?
Answer: It is due to the seeds of consciousnesses accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Because it follows after the concentration that is without vitarka and vicāra,
once one has arisen from that [concentration], this [state] manifests before one;
and so on, as explained at length.
3. Sevenfold Classification.
Now, it is classified by way of ten gates.
First, the determination of its essential nature.
Second, the aspects;
third, the explanation of the names;
fourth, the establishment and exclusion [of categories].
Fifth, they are subsumed within the eight consciousnesses.
Sixth, some are untainted (anāsrava).
Seventh, they take the three periods of time as their objects.
The eight and ten types of mental scattering (*vikṣepa*) are subsumed within the ten types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Chapter Nine concerns the stage of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). Chapter Ten is the section on questions and answers concerning the primary and secondary aspects of vitarka and vicāra.
The fifth [chapter], the Yoga of the Flowing Stream, concerns the names of activities sought through:
essence, object, practice, and motivation; distinctions and definitive analysis; conduct, contact, leading, and association.
Vitarka (initial inquiry) and vicāra (sustained investigation) are analyzed by way of seven categories:
first, their essential nature;
second, their objects of focus.
Third, the aspects;
fourth, the origination;
fifth, the distinctions.
Sixth, the determination;
seventh, the circulation.
Regarding the nature of the essence:
Not deeply investigating and deliberating is its essential nature;
if it does involve deep investigation and deliberation, wisdom (*prajñā*) is its essential nature.
As for the two objects of focus:
It takes the meaning of the sets of names, phrases, and syllables as its object.
Regarding the three modes of activity:
the mode of seeking is vitarka (applied thought).
Investigative activity is investigation (*vitarka*).
As for the four modes of origination,
they refer to the utterance of speech.
The fivefold differentiation refers to the seven types of discrimination.
The sixfold definitive analysis refers to—
If one asks whether vitarka and vicāra are themselves discrimination (*vikalpa*),
[the answer is: if vitarka and vicāra are both discrimination,
there is also discrimination that is not vitarka or vicāra.
This refers to all remaining minds and mental factors of the three realms in comparison to the supramundane path.
Regarding the seven types of transmigration,
each of the five destinies is subject to six questions.
Just as with the applied thought and sustained thought in the hells:
what are their modes of activity? What do they contact?
What is it that induces?
What is it associated with?
What is it sought after?
What karma functions?
This applies likewise even when asking about the applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) of the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, in the hells, it functions as a state of dejection (*daurmanasya*).
Contacting an unpleasing object gives rise to suffering and is associated with mental distress.
Constantly seeking liberation,
yet with a mind afflicted by the turning of karma,
one experiences exclusively painful sensations.
The same applies to the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Those in the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*), the human realm (*manuṣyagati*), and the hungry ghosts of great power (*maharddhika-preta*) are for the most part engaged in sorrowful conduct.
There is a slight inclination toward joyful conduct,
but one mostly encounters what is unlovely,
while only rarely encountering objects of affection.
For the most part it induces suffering;
for a small portion it induces pleasure;
and it is mostly associated with mental distress.
They are associated with a slight degree of joy;
for the most part they seek liberation from suffering,
and only to a small extent do they seek the encounter with pleasure.
The karma of an afflicted mind proceeds as follows:
the vitarka and vicāra of the gods in the desire realm are for the most part associated with joyful activity,
and to a lesser extent with sorrowful activity.
It is mostly pleasant to touch and rarely unpleasant to touch;
it mostly induces happiness.
It involves little suffering and is mostly associated with joy,
with only a small degree of association with grief.
For the most part, they seek the pleasure of encounter;
for the least part, they seek liberation from suffering.
Thus, their minds are afflicted as karma unfolds.
The stage of the first dhyāna is exclusively characterized by inclination toward joy,
exclusively directed toward desirable objects,
and exclusively conducing to pleasure.
Constantly accompanied by joy,
he seeks only not to be separated from bliss;
his mental karma proceeds without affliction.
Fifteen unique karmas.
The verse says:
Discrimination, examination of the object, intoxication, madness, dreaming, waking, and fainting.
Awakening, initiating karma, detachment from desire, falling away, abandoning, reconnecting, birth, and death—
these are the fifteen unique functions of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as explained in the first discourse on yoga.
First is the object of investigation through discrimination,
which consists of the seven types of discrimination;
second is the object of investigation through deliberation.
That is to say: those induced by the appropriate, the inappropriate, and that which is neither;
third, intoxication;
fourth, insanity.
Five dreams,
six awakenings,
and seven faintings.
Eight, awakening;
nine, the ability to initiate bodily and vocal karma;
ten, freedom from desire.
Eleventh, falling away from detachment;
twelfth, severing the roots of goodness;
thirteenth, reconnecting the roots of goodness.
14. Birth; 15. Death. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter 2.
Śāriputra said: "Now, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never heard before, all my doubts and regrets have been severed.
That verse further says: "I have attained the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya)."
Hearing also removes sorrow and affliction; doubt and regret are themselves misdeeds (*duṣkṛta*).
It is also aversion.
Wisdom is always accompanied by non-attachment.
Doubt is doubt regarding the facts;
it is the uncertainty that one will not become a Buddha.
Sorrow is precisely remorse.
Because one regrets former evil;
regret is itself doubt.
Herein, it is right reflection.
If their essence were vitarka and they were pervasive across the untainted (anāsrava),
why would the five faculties among the fifty-seven and twenty-two faculties not include the six factors among the thirty-seven [limbs of enlightenment]?
That is to say: speech, action, livelihood, joy, tranquility, and equanimity.
Therefore, right thought is distinct [from the other factors] and is specifically the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
Since this master discusses cause and effect comprehensively, its essence is wisdom itself.
The former master’s view may be considered correct;
therefore, vitarka is not without outflows (anāsrava),
as it is designated by the name "vitarka."
Just as the gratification within the three realms is called "pleasure," the fourth *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"If the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) is comprised within the conditioned meditative concentrations (*samāpatti*), such as the first dhyāna..."
It is also called "with vitarka and vicāra," because one enters this meditative absorption by taking suchness as its object based on dharmas that serve as the basis for vitarka and vicāra;
it is not due to the active manifestation of conceptual discrimination.
Therefore, it is known that vitarka and vicāra induce the outflow-free (anāsrava).

Regarding the outflow-free inducing the intermediate [state], both interpretations are permissible. If one says that vitarka and vicāra are necessarily conceptualization (vikalpa), yet it is not definitively stated that they belong exclusively to the third [dhyāna], they thus also pertain to the outflow-free.
Why not analyze this by means of the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*)?
This is because they differ in their mutual breadth and narrowness. Regarding "repentance, detachment from desire, and relinquishment," see the second chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Śāriputra said: "From the past until now, throughout both day and night, I have constantly reproached myself;
yet today, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never before heard, all my doubts and regrets have been severed."
"Regret" (kaukṛtya) refers to doubt regarding the Dharma;
it is not an affliction (kleśa).
This is stated in the Fifty-sixth [Treatise].
There are three types of bodily activity:
namely, inhalation, exhalation, and physical action.
There are likewise three types of vocal activity.
This refers to vitarka, vicāra, and vocal karma; because right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa) and speech are its designations.
Vitarka is also associated with the outflow-free (anāsrava); thus there are fifty-seven.

Among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), three are not included within the five faculties (pañcendriya): namely, vocal karma, livelihood (ājīva), joy (prīti), tranquility (praśrabdhi), and equanimity (upekṣā).
Since it is not stated that right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is not included within wisdom (*prajñā*), how is this to be reconciled?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56, states:
"There are three types of bodily activity."
These are inhalation and exhalation, as well as bodily action.
Verbal formations are also threefold:
namely, vitarka, vicāra, and verbal action.
Mental formations are also threefold:
namely, feeling (vedanā), volition (cetanā), and mental action (manaskarma).
Therefore, what prevents speech from proceeding even when the Buddha is without vitarka and vicāra?
Because karma is not non-existent, although the two breaths and so forth are absent within the fourth dhyāna, the body remains established.
Furthermore, since the two meditative states lack vitarka and vicāra as well as vocal karma, speech should also continue to function; this is because [karma] is both universal and non-universal.
As previously stated,
bodily action (kāyakarman) is exclusively defiled and cannot serve as an analogy.
Furthermore, the treatise merely cites defiled bodily action for the sake of illustration.
In reality, there are also untainted wholesome dharmas [in the Buddha’s body].
If this were not so, how could the Buddha’s body and speech function?
Therefore, it is through the volition of karma that they are set in motion.
Because they constantly enter the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the mental factors that arise together, the verse says:
Five factors arise together with five; Nine factors necessarily arise with six.
Nine factors necessarily [arise with] fourteen; twenty-one, fifteen, and three factors arise with sixteen;
eight factors arise with seventeen—all these are associated with mental concomitants (citta-samprayukta). One who possesses wisdom should reflect upon this.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 57, among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), it is asked:
"Based on which faculty did the Blessed One speak these words:
'It travels far and wanders alone'?"
"Sleeping bodiless in a cave.
The answer is: it depends on the locus of the mental faculty (*manas*), because the prior limit is beginningless.
It is called "far-reaching" because it universally takes all objects of knowledge as its cognitive domain;
it is so called because each moment in the continuum of the mind proceeds one after another.
Because it is without a sovereign,
it is called "solitary.
Because it is formless, invisible, and non-obstructive, it is so named.
It is called "bodiless.
Because it relies upon form, it is said to "sleep in a cave. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, fascicle 4, states:
"Because it ranges through all objects of cognition."
It is called "Far-Reaching.
To demonstrate this meaning,
it further states "Solitary Traveling."
Because there is no second [self],
it is said to be "without body"; because it lacks form and substance, it is "without body."
Because it sleeps in a cave and because it dwells within, it is called "to tame" this [mind],
for one exercises mastery over such a mind.
Those whose minds are difficult to tame are so because their natures are stubborn and unruly;
the Sthavira school maintains that there is an intermediate state (antarābhava).

How can it be said that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) necessarily gives rise to the defilements that moisten rebirth? This is because the initial position held that there was no intermediate state, whereas the final position holds that there is.
The textual principles for this should be examined within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The fruition of non-conceptualization (*āsaṃjñika-vipāka*) excludes the courses of conduct (*airyāpathika*),
because one enters meditative absorption while in the causal state,
and because it is difficult for the fruit to arise [from such a state].
The syllogism of *vijñapti-mātra* established by our Preceptor states:
"That which is truly established as form is not separate from visual consciousness."

Because it is admitted by [the opponent] himself to be included in the first three [realms] while not being included by the eye, just like visual consciousness; this contradicts the definitive position of the Master Śubhagupta, who states:
"Color is truly established."
It is definitely distinct from eye-consciousness,
because [the Vaibhāṣikas] themselves admit that it is included within the first three [bases] but does not include eye-consciousness,
just like the eye-faculty; this is as explained in Master Jing’s *Jiaojie* (Excerpts and Explanations).
From the section on the knowledge of others' minds in Master Yu’s work,
one should cite the explanation of Master Sthiramati regarding the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
In the eighty-ninth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are eight types of appropriation (*upādāna*).
The first two are internal and external;
the latter six are established by means of the six groups of six phenomena (*ṣaṭ-ṣaṭ-dharma*).
Therefore, it was verified later and recorded as a marginal note in the third section of the preceding treatise. However,

regarding the statement that "the non-returner (anāgāmin), due to the strength of the power of the antidote, does not give rise to afflictions and so forth at the stage of being moistened for rebirth":
Among these, there are five difficulties.
Taking the fifth question as the first and the second [question] as the second should be done.
The first becomes the third;
the rest follow in order. One question:
as stated in [Treatise] 59, "the vision of the truths (satyadarśana) is moistened solely by the latent tendencies (anuśaya)."
The noble ones (*ārya*) also moisten [the seeds] through their manifest activity (*samudācāra*).

Since it has already been stated that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) moisten both seeds and manifest activity, it follows that ordinary beings should possess moisture consisting solely of seeds. Answer: For the noble ones, there is much gradual reduction [of defilements], and thus their moisture involves manifest activity.

Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and others [possess] [seeds], there are not merely seeds [that produce rebirth]. Furthermore, it would follow that when an Ārya is born in another stage (*bhūmi*), he would only moisten rebirth through seeds;
if he were born in his own stage, he would do so by means of manifest activity (*samudācāra*).
Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should also be treated in the same way.

If, when born in their own stage, [the seeds] can be moistened because the counteractive path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) has not yet arisen, then when born in another stage, they should only be moistened by seeds. This current interpretation is not correct.
When the untainted path is complete,
its power surpasses the afflictions;
when the untainted path is incomplete, it does not.
Alternatively, it may manifest as being powerful;
however, because this is not the case for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it cannot serve as a precedent. This constitutes the second objection.
The noble ones of the first and second fruits possess the moisture of their own stage in both its manifest and latent forms.
Regarding the meaning of the non-returner being born in their own place, it should likewise possess manifest moisture. Answer:
This is possible, as it conforms to the case of the first and second fruits.
As with the cases of those who are non-returners (*anāgāmin*) in various places,
the treatise omits these for brevity.
Furthermore, such reasoning is untenable.
Because the first and second fruits have not yet attained the complete path,
they can utilize present [moistening];
because the third fruit has already attained the complete path, it does not.
Even if one is born into one’s own stage (*svabhūmi*), it is still only the seeds that are moistened.
This is because the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Treatise Five) states that they are moistened by means of active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Furthermore, only the first two fruits [of the path] are said to function through active manifestations. Third, the objection.

Why is it that for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) there is both the moistening of the manifest and the moistening of the seeds, whereas for noble ones (*ārya*) there is only the moistening of the seeds?
Is it because the seeds are stronger than those [manifest states]? Answer: Because the karma of the noble ones is determinate (*niyata*).
Strong karma can exist as a seed alone;

the karma of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is not thus, and therefore it may manifest in actual activity (*samudācāra*). Question: If that is so, then the karma of the first two fruits would also already be determined.
[Question: Should it not be that [the seeds] are moistened by the seeds alone? [Answer: Generally, when one is born into suffering and oppressed, wholesome karma is weak;
it must rely on its actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) in order to be moistened.
For the Noble Ones (*ārya*), however, birth involves little suffering and their wholesome karma is superior.
Because it moistens the seeds alone,
and because the untainted can also support the tainted,
it is not the same as that of ordinary beings.
Furthermore, ordinary beings do not perceive whether [the karma] produced is much or little;
they merely rely on the manifestation of afflictions, wherein both seeds and manifest states all provide assistance and moisture.
Noble ones, however, know that the amount of karma is fixed.
By this, only the seeds are moistened. Regarding the four difficulties:
that which is suppressed by the six practices does not suppress the moisture that gives rise to greed and so forth;
it only suppresses greed and so forth directed toward scattered objects.

Question: For what reason do ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who have attained meditative concentration not moisten [their karma] to be reborn in a lower realm, yet their karma causes them to be born in other planes of existence? Answer: Because they rely on auxiliary factors such as craving (tṛṣṇā), they are able to moisten [the karma] for rebirth.
Since those companions have already perished, his strength is too weak to moisten [the realm] alone;
for this reason, he does not descend to a lower plane.
Furthermore, it is generally the case that by performing new karma of superior quality, one is reborn in a higher realm.
The noble ones arise from past karma.
When the seeds exist, they are born in that realm, just as ordinary persons in the desire realm possess the karma for all five destinies;
whichever karma is predominant is the first to manifest.
Therefore, although inferior karma is not absent,
superior karma— being more excellent than the former— goes first;
this is unless the superior karma is weak.
To resolve this, it is said that they are later reborn;
having fallen away from the higher meditative attainments (*dhyāna*), they are born within their own realm.
Thus, there is no fault regarding the five difficulties.
Why is it not admitted that the co-arising view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and other such afflictions among the six consciousnesses cannot be suppressed even by attaining the worldly path,
nor can they be severed even upon attaining the third fruit?

Question: Does the obstruction at the upper limit resemble that of the seventh consciousness? Answer: No, because that [obstruction] obstructs both the fruit and its emergence from its own stage (*svabhūmi*), whereas the subtle [obstruction] of the seventh consciousness does not obstruct either the fruit or its emergence from its own stage.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the twelfth [chapter], concerning the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
states: "Because one has previously well-cultivated and purified the mind,
one does not conceptually differentiate the characteristics and marks of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)."
One is able to enter this meditative absorption and emerge from it;
through extensive cultivation,
one is able to enter and emerge from it spontaneously.
Upon emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation, one contacts two kinds of contact:
first, the immovable;
second, that of nothingness.
Third, the signless (*animitta*).
At the time of emerging from meditative absorption, one generally emerges from that concentration by means of three objects.
First, by means of an object possessing signs (*sanimitta*).
Second, by way of the object;
third, by way of the cessation of the object;
through these, one sequentially experiences three types of contact.
When emerging from meditative absorption while having an object as a condition,
there is no conceit that agitates the mind by thinking "this is I," nor does one conceive of a future self, such as "I shall exist," and so forth.
Therefore, it is the contact of immovability.
When one emerges from meditative absorption while taking an object as a condition,
there is that which consists of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
Therefore, one definitely enters the contact of non-existence (*akiṃcanyāyatana-sparśa*).
At the time of emerging from meditative absorption by taking the state of cessation (*nirodha*) as the object,
there is no mental engagement with any signs (*nimitta*).
Because it takes the signless realm as its object,
it is said that "it touches the signless touch. This means that after emerging from meditative absorption,
it takes the three objects as its objects.
That which has an object consists of the five conditioned aggregates;
it is the mind that enters meditative absorption by relying on the characteristic of non-perception and now emerges from it.
That which has cessation as its object is the mind that enters meditative absorption by relying on the characteristic of cessation and now emerges from it.
Beyond these two, there is no third affliction;
therefore, contact is non-existent, and the name "contact" refers to the object as its condition.
This leads to the subsequent indeterminate [state].

The mind emerging from that [meditative absorption] does not correspond to the one that entered, because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is distinct. Alternatively, when it emerges from concentration by taking the six sense objects as its object, it is collectively termed "object-of-object" (*ālambanālambana*);
this refers exclusively to the object of an object.
This explains emerging from meditative absorption spontaneously and with mastery.
Even if one emerges from absorption without mastery while perceiving objects,
although there is no textual statement to that effect, it does not exceed these three [modes].
Question: Why do fainting (*mūrchā*) and sleep (*middha*) both induce a state without mind (*acittaka*)?
Question: Since there is indeed the substance of the object-field of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) [in the case of sleep], why is it not the same for sleep?
If there is a mental factor (*caitta*) of sleep, is there not likewise one of lethargy (*styāna*)?

When there is a state of mental lethargy, what is this lethargy? It is that which arises from the intensification of the contact of lethargy (*styāna-saṃsparśa*), thereby inducing the state of lethargy.

Because the various mental states (*caitasika*) are induced by different degrees of *middha* (torpor) to arise in distinct stages, there is no separate mental factor of "dejection" (*daurmanasya*). Why is *middha* not considered an object of contact (*spraṣṭavya*)? That which is capable of inducing mental factors is precisely the category of *middha*.
Because that which induces the sensation of suffocation is itself mental suffocation,
it does not exist [as a separate entity].
"Suffocation" (styāna) may also refer to torpor (middha).
Because of its lack of functional capacity,
or because of fainting, it is conventionally designated upon the basis of the five aggregates,
just as the term "fainting" is applied to those born in the formless realms within the cycle of birth and death.
These are the six factors associated with the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
Five are without mind;
three exist in only one realm.
That is to say, sleep belongs exclusively to the desire realm;
the attainment of non-conception and birth belong exclusively to the form realm;
one [state] pervades all three realms.
That is to say, it is "stupefaction. First, there is that which is not a realm (*dhātu*), namely the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Two arise from only one realm:
namely, sleep and the state of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñika).
One arises from both realms.
That is to say, the attainment of non-conception arises throughout the three realms; it is characterized by a state of stupor.
It pervades the three realms yet does not arise from within those realms;
this refers to the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), as it also arises in the Pure Land.
Two are exclusively wholesome,
namely the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Three are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This refers to the remaining three.
There are two types of aspects (ākāra):
first, the aspect of the reflected image is called an aspect.
Why is it that [the aspect] resembles its original object?

Why are the two seeing-aspects (*darśana-bhāga*) called "modes of activity" (*ākāra*), while [the objective aspect] does not resemble [the object]? Answer: The mental image (*pratibimba*) is called the mode of activity.
Regarding the characteristics of the aspect of apprehension (darśana-bhāga) as an act of cognition:
the activity of the aspect of apprehension is merely the appearance of the object;
thus, the aspect of apprehension is termed the "aspect of cognition" (ākāra).
Because it operates within the substance of the object,
like non-conceptual wisdom which lacks any formal characteristics,
it may appear similar or dissimilar.

Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that the aspect of the mental image (*pratibimba*) always resembles its object, for conditions such as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) do not resemble [their objects].
Answer: There are six types of equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).
First, answering by following the meaning of another's position;
second, answering by citing one's own correct principle;
third, answering that consciousness arises without beginning.

1. The answer that accords with the examples; 2. The answer that clarifies the Dharma through the parable of the finger; 3. The answer that distinguishes by means of subtle principles. 4. The answer that accords with the mind through examples; 5. The answer that reveals the Dharma through the parable of the finger;
6. The answer that distinguishes by means of subtle principles.
"The three realms are mind-only.
This clarifies consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) by relying on contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
Furthermore, it is taught that the objects of cognition are manifestations of consciousness-only.
By stating that objects arise from the mind, one clarifies *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).
Furthermore, by stating that all phenomena do not depart from the mind,
one reveals *vijñaptimātra* based on their non-separation [from it].
This single gateway alone fully encompasses all phenomena.
Furthermore, it is taught that sentient beings follow the defilement and purity of their minds;
based on internal maturation (*vipāka*), it clarifies the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Furthermore, it is said that a bodhisattva who has accomplished the four wisdoms clarifies *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) by relying on the cultivation of its causes.
Moreover, a verse from the *Gāthā* states: "The objects of the mind, the intellect, and consciousness," and so forth.
Furthermore, that which is the object of cognition is also termed "consciousness-only.
Among the four wisdoms, the first contemplates only the object,
while the second contemplates only the wisdom itself.
The three pairs consist of the observation of objects and the mind;
furthermore, the first pair refutes only the Sarvāstivāda,
while the second refutes only the Sautrāntika.
The latter two [sections] refute both [positions].
Within the critique regarding direct perception contradicting the tenet,
one should also cite the Sarvāstivāda, the Saṃmitīya, and the Mahāsāṃghika schools.
Furthermore, taking up the mind of another vehicle is difficult;
this should also be briefly cited in the commentary.
When the light of a lamp extends its radiance to that [object], [it reaches it].
This contradicts the second [point] of the Abhidharma.
The refutation states: "Just as a lamp-light is emitted instantaneously, so too is sound.
Consult the *Chao* (Excerpts).
The "Radiating Light" refers to the gateway that accords with principle;
it suddenly brings forth the meaning of the Mahāyāna,
namely, for those ordinary beings who seek the fruit of Buddhahood.
After attaining meditative concentration in the form realm, one subsequently induces the outflow-free state;
for such a person must necessarily be born in the Palace of Great Sovereignty (*Maheśvara*) in the Pure Abodes (*Śuddhāvāsa*) to attain enlightenment.
Herein, it is asked:
The fourth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
Within the four dhyānas, there are heavens where ordinary beings and noble ones dwell together;
each is born there according to whether their cultivation was of the weak, medium, or superior grade.
The Heaven of Non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva) is subsumed within the Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala) and has no separate location.
Furthermore, there are various noble ones who dwell in the five distinct Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), namely:
the Unafflicted (avṛha), the Heatless (atapa), the Clearly Manifest (sudṛśa), the Good-to-See (sudarśana), and the Ultimate Form (akaniṣṭha).
By means of practicing the fourth dhyāna through the mixed cultivation of the inferior, middling, superior, superior-excellent, and supreme categories,
there is furthermore a place beyond the Pure Abodes where Mahāmaheśvara dwells.
Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are born therein due to their extreme cultivation.
Now, examining the meaning and intent,
there are four permutations regarding those who take birth through the cultivation of meditative concentration and so forth.
First, there is only the permeation of the out-flowing (sāsrava).
As stated in the eighth [chapter], this involves the relinquishing of merit, life-span, and karmic formations,
as well as birth in each of the three locations within the four dhyānas of the *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented death and rebirth).
The treatise mentions only "perfuming" (*vāsanā*) and does not mention "mixed cultivation" (*miśra-bhāvanā*).

Therefore, the twelfth [verse] states that others take mixed cultivation to be born in the five Pure Abodes (*pañca-śuddhāvāsa*), but does not say they are born below them. There is cultivation that is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
Just as with all transformative births and deaths (saṃvartanīya-jarāmaraṇa),
there is a mixed cultivation of both the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) and the outflow-free (anāsrava),
namely, that of those born in the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).
The twelfth yoga states:
"Suppose there is someone who has already attained the four dhyānas, both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
and enters these various dhyānas in a continuous succession over a long period of time."
The contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states alternate and intermingle with one another;
even to the point where the uncontaminated manifests immediately after the contaminated,
and the contaminated re-enters immediately after the uncontaminated.
One should know that the cultivation [of these practices] is perfected up to this point;
for by this, one attains mastery over meditative concentration (samādhi),
which is the fruit of mastery over meditative attainment (samāpatti).
Thus, the dwelling in happiness in the present life becomes increasingly clear and pure.
Furthermore, by means of this, one attains the path of non-retrogression.
Moreover, it is the path that leads to the purification and cultivation of superior qualities, such as the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
If there are those who pass away while still possessing further grasping (*upādāna*),
they enter the Śuddhāvāsa heavens by virtue of this causal condition;
it is not said that they are born into the lower dhyānas.
By relying on this cultivation, one causes the previously created karma of the lower three heavens to become increasingly superior,
resulting in rebirth in the five Pure Abodes;
it is not new karma of the present that can induce such maturation.
Because the Noble Ones do not create karma.
Since it is stated that the fourth [ground] involves the ultimate cultivation of the tenth ground, one is born there from the tenth ground.
Furthermore, from the eighth ground onward, one undergoes birth through the transformation of support (*pariṇāmiki-jāti*).
How is it that through further cultivation in the ten stages one is born there? This refers to those who have already been born in the three lower heavens of the fourth dhyāna at the eighth stage;
now, by means of extremely pure, untainted, and superior karma—surpassing the karma of the previous three stages—they are able to be born there through the influence of this present karma.
In reality, it is not a new birth.
Because one proceeds toward the place where the fruit of karma belonging to that same level (*bhūmi*) is to be experienced, it is called "birth" (*jāti*);
thus, "birth" is defined as being of the same level.
They are called "those who go" because they proceed to different realms;

this is not contradictory. The fourth category consists of those not supported by either [of the two aforementioned types] for their birth, namely all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because the mind of one in the form realm remains fixed upon its object through the power of karma, it is called "immovable" (*aniñjya*);

it is not called immovable because it does not experience [rebirth] in a different location. Since it is stated that the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is the master of the four dhyānas, [this refers to that state].
Ten kinds of fruit-signs arise in the Palace of Sovereignty;
because one must manifest upon the great precious lotus seat, one necessarily attains birth there,
rather than having already attained birth there at the eighth stage.
This is because it is taught that [the transformation of the basis] occurs only at the tenth stage through extreme cultivation;
furthermore, because Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage are not the masters of that [transformation],
nor is there birth and death through the transformation of support (pariṇāma-vipariṇāma) for them.
Even if one were to grant that death and birth exist, which new karma would produce them?
It cannot be said that the seventh consciousness first arises in a particular realm before being born into another,
because its arising is not determinate.
If it is said that there is no turning of the mind in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
its initial arising occurs only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If it is said that there is a turning of the mind in the form realm, [its initial arising may also occur there].
It first arises as a supernormal power (abhijñā) pertaining to the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
because it does not abide in meditative concentration (samādhi) and because it first arises from the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā).
If this equality first arises within the body of the form realm (rūpadhātu),
the untainted seeds (anāsravabīja) reside in consciousness,
and the five untainted sense objects (viṣaya) exist internally as substantial transformations.

The eighth [consciousness] does not take any as its object; that is to say, because the five uncontaminated faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) serve as the supports for the five consciousnesses, the eighth [consciousness] does not take them as objects.
What fault is there in this? The explanation says:
If the five faculties are substantial, the eighth consciousness necessarily takes them as its object;
if they are provisional, it is not necessary for the eighth consciousness to take form as its object.
Likewise, seeds, form, and so forth do not require the eight conditions to constitute their actual utility.
Therefore, within the causal stage, there are no untainted (*anāsrava*) five faculties. Question: It may be so for form and the other [objects].

But how can the eighth consciousness, which does not take [them] as objects, become a real seed? Just as associated dharmas and the sixth consciousness—which both take [objects] as conditions—are not real seeds, why must the eighth consciousness necessarily have the function of being a real seed through taking [objects] as conditions?
This point should be considered:
the claim that an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) must necessarily have an existing entity as its object contradicts [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] 52.
Regarding the statement that "it arises from the mind conditioned by those [objects]," one should reconcile it as follows:
the five consciousnesses must necessarily have a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana*).

This refers to cases where, through the power of karma, or by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the five sense-objects are transformed within a particular realm or stage (*dhātu-bhūmi*).
It is not necessarily the case that there must be an essential nature [in the object], such as when one born in a higher realm takes as an object the form of a lower realm;

or when one whose body is in a lower realm gives rise to the divine eye or ear to take as objects the forms and so forth of a higher realm. Furthermore, it is explained that the mind of maturation (*vipāka*) has a superficial and shallow engagement with its objects.
It does not necessarily require a substantial basis (*bimba*).
Although the eighth consciousness takes what resembles another's body as its object,
it is still not termed a "substantial basis."
Because the first five consciousnesses and so forth possess discrimination, they necessarily rely upon an objective essence (*vastu*).
Even when they take an object belonging to a different stage (*bhūmi*), although there is no objective essence for their own foundational consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), [they still require one].

Because that which undergoes transformation by another serves as its objective basis (*ālambana*). If that were so, then the preceding six consciousnesses would [likewise] have no time when they lack an objective basis,
because they are constantly engaged in conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
The former explanation is superior: the five consciousnesses are coarse because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are easily known;
they are dull because their modes of activity are shallow and non-continuous;
and they are inferior because they arise only when induced by others.
Because they do not arise through their own power;
"the fundamental consciousness and so forth" refers to that which is transformed by the sixth consciousness.
Because the "presently existing" (dai-shitsu) faculty penetrates both the derivative and the fundamental,
it is here explained according to its fundamental nature;
thus, among the twenty-two faculties:
How many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)? Answer: Four—namely, male-female, grief, and suffering—and a portion of fifteen.

Excluding the three untainted (*anāsrava*) and the aforementioned four. How many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)? Answer: A portion of fifteen. How many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)? Answer: A portion of eight.

When the mind relinquishes life, [how many] among faith and the other five [faculties] are unconditioned? Answer: Three are untainted; nine are partially so. How many are bound to the desire realm, taking the desire realm as their object? Answer: Four.
Two are bound to the desire and form realms;
their meaning is that they are bound to the desire realm.
Three are bound to both the desire and form realms.
It takes the two realms as its referent:
those bound to the desire realm and the form realm, as well as those that are unbound.
It takes all that is bound and unbound as its referent.
The seven [categories] consist of those bound to the three realms and those unbound;
their meaning is that all are both bound and unbound.
One [category] consists of those bound to the form realm and those unbound.

All [the faculties] have "objects" as their meaning. Second, those that are not bound have "all" as their meaning. Question: What is the meaning of the five material sense-faculties? Answer: They each have their own distinct objects, such as visible form and so forth. Question: What is the meaning of the sixth faculty? Answer: It has all phenomena (dharmas) as its object. Question: What is the meaning of the male and female faculties? Answer: Because they are associated with desire, they are subsumed under contact (*sparśa*). Question: What is the meaning of the five feeling faculties?
The faculties of suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity correspond to the meaning of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

What is the meaning of the faculties of faith and so forth? They pertain to all objects that are to be attained or abandoned. The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*) is that which exerts no slackening regarding both attainment and abandonment. The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) is the non-forgetful retention of what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated. What is the meaning of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)?
Answer: Regarding the faculties of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, what is the meaning of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)?
Regarding the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), what is its meaning?
For one who cultivates clear realization (*abhisamaya*), from the stage of desire for wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*) onwards, throughout all paths of skillful means (*upāyamārga*).
The meaning of those five faculties is precisely the meaning of this faculty.

The meaning of the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) refers to the five faculties from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).

This is the meaning of these faculties: the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) encompasses the meaning of the five faculties from the initial path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) up until the entry into nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).

This is the meaning of these faculties; it is clarified through cultivation according to [the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] chapter sixty-nine, as well as the ninth, tenth, and thirteenth chapters of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*.
This should be analyzed in detail:

prior to the stages (bhūmi), one attains both types of cultivation—cultivation by practice (ābhisamskārika) and cultivation by acquisition (prāyogika)—which are with outflows (sāsrava); at the stage of attainment alone, one cultivates only that which is without outflows (anāsrava).
If one is on the path of seeing,
there is the acquisition and practice cultivation of the untainted,
and the acquisition cultivation of the tainted.
Prior to the seventh bhūmi, both types of cultivation are both contaminated and uncontaminated;
from the eighth bhūmi onward, both types of cultivation are exclusively uncontaminated.
One attains the cultivation of the out-flowing (sāsrava).
This is because one receives the status of the ten kings.
As for supramundane wisdom (lokottara-jñāna) and mundane-supramundane wisdom (laukika-lokottara-jñāna):
Having already distinguished the cultivation [of the antidotes] both in the higher and lower stages,
as well as the practiced and unpracticed [levels],
at what stage do they arise and when do they not?
All of this should be considered according to reason, because the four roots of goodness do not exist within the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

Since it is stated that they exist during the untainted path of seeing (*anāsrava-darśana-mārga*), one should know that they are cultivated as having been previously acquired [in the mundane stage]. This refers to the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātendriya*) in the Abhidharma.
There may be ten or nine faculties; when the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is included therein, it is then associated with the outflows (*sāsrava*).

Furthermore, the outflow-tainted faculties of faith and so forth, during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), also constitute the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
In this context, although the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is excluded,
why are the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) not also excluded?

If it is argued that all outflow-tainted states are excluded because there is no sorrow, then since the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) has already excluded the faculty of sorrow...
One should likewise not grasp at other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*). Since one already grasps all such contaminated things, this case should be no different.
Furthermore, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is characterized by a mind of deep longing, and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is likewise so.
These faculties are with outflows (sāsrava) and inferior to those without outflows (anāsrava);
it is the latter that are truly faculties.
This is according to the actual reality.
The outflow-tainted [faculties] are also included; however,
setting aside the inferior and taking up the superior,
only the outflow-free [faculties] are designated as the faculty of "already known."
When the faculty of final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is established as that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it then encompasses the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*);
yet, because it functions as a dominant faculty (*indriya-adhipati*), it does not grasp what is outflow-tainted.
That which is outflow-tainted refers to faith and the other [faculties].
It is not called the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātendriya*). The faculty of one who has already known (*ājñendriya*) should also be understood according to this same text,
because it is said to be untainted (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, those that are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) are also included among those to be abandoned. The meaning of "predominance" (*ādhipatya*) is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*).
How is the meaning of predominance established as a faculty?
It is for the purpose of manifesting [the predominance] over various respective objects.
Because each respective phenomenon possesses the most preeminent meaning;
it is not that a single faculty has a dominant influence over all phenomena.
This indicates that within each distinct phenomenon, there exists a state of supreme excellence.
Therefore, they are established as faculties (*indriya*). Second, the establishment and exclusion [of the faculties]. Fifty-seven.
Eighth, another sequence for explaining the establishment and exclusion.
Apprehending objects;
the six continuities of the family;
and the two means of livelihood.
First, the fruition of karma;
fifth, the mundane;
and fifth, the supramundane purity.
Third, based on this measure, the faculties are established;
they are able to experience manifest and hidden objects,
and constitute the limit of the time of experience.
The first [faculty] experiences the object and gives rise to defilement;
the five [faculties] establish purification;

and the final faculty is the basis of the mind. This is their distinction, this is their abiding, this is their defilement, this is their equipment, and this is their purification—it is by these measures that the faculties are established. Third, as for the conventional and the real:
Sixteen are real;
six are not real. These are:
male, female, life-force, and the three untainted [faculties].
A small portion of the male and female faculties,
as well as the life faculty, are nominally existent because they are seeds of the mind-faculty.
A portion of the three untainted faculties and nine faculties [are also nominally existent].
Therefore, regarding the six provisional categories— the fourfold classification of mind, mental factors, matter, non-associated formations, and unconditioned phenomena—
the seven types of matter consist of the five [faculties] such as the eye, as well as male and female.
One mind refers to the mental faculty (manas).
Three minor factors.
The three portions of the untainted (*anāsrava*) and ten mental factors (*caitasika*) that are entirely wholesome;
that is to say, the five sensations (*vedanā*), the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and portions of the three untainted faculties (*indriya*).
First, the dissociated [factors],
namely the life-faculty;
all conditioned phenomena.
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is not a faculty. Among the five [faculties], how many are wholesome?
Eight are exclusively wholesome;
namely, the five beginning with faith and the three untainted (anāsrava) faculties.
Eight are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
namely, the seven material faculties and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
One faculty is common to both the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the unwholesome (*akuśala*).

That is to say, the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*). Five faculties pertain to all three moral natures—that is, the four sensations (*vedanā*) and the mental faculty (*manas*). Of these six, how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Four are exclusively of the desire realm:
namely, masculinity, femininity, grief, and suffering.
Fifteen are partial.
This refers to the five material faculties, the mind faculty, the life faculty, the three feelings, and the five beginning with faith—
excluding the three untainted faculties.
These constitute fifteen factors that are partially bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Eight [roots] are associated with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu):

namely, the five beginning with faith, the mind-root, the life-root, and three untainted roots (anāsrava-indriya). Nine roots are not bound (aniyata) by way of their parts. How many of these are obtainable in the preliminary stage (anāgamya)? Seven.
Answer: Eleven.
The mind faculty, the faculty of joy, the faculty of equanimity, the five beginning with faith, and the three untainted faculties—these eighteen faculties can be obtained in the first dhyāna.
Excluding sorrow, suffering, male, and female.
The second absorption is likewise.
In the third absorption, there are seventeen.
Excluding the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), there are sixteen in the fourth dhyāna; excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
there are eleven in the first three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
That is to say: the faculties of life, mind, and equanimity; the five beginning with faith; the three untainted faculties;
and the eight [faculties] excluding the three untainted faculties.

In the eighth fascicle, regarding seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, as in the first commentary on the Abhidharma: although within these two eyes there are those that are not superior seeds capable of producing fruit, these two are termed "projecting" (*ākṣepa*) and "arising" (*abhinirvṛtti*).

The meaning of the ten causes is established because the distinction between the moistened and the unmoistened is made manifest through the attainment of results, and because the continuity [of the stream] remains uninterrupted.
As stated in a separate chapter,
the sixty-sixth [section] clarifying phenomena that have causes says:
"Furthermore, there are the various karmas and afflictions previously committed."
Within the three realms, the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is preeminent.

This fruit of maturation is called a "conditioned phenomenon with a cause" because it is produced by the causes of karma and afflictions; however, this is not the sixth among the ten causes, namely the "causal production cause" (*abhinirvṛttihetu*).

The *Pravṛttihetu-śāstra* does not state that it produces a distinct ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*). This [term] refers to the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*) in contrast to the determining cause (*niyamahetu*) and others.
As appropriate, the term "projecting cause" is applied metaphorically to the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) with respect to its fulfillment of a distinct fruit.
Because they are induced by coarse characteristics,
and because they are explained in relation to the fulfillment of the fruit and the fulfillment of the cause,
there are six kinds of contradictions.
Thirty-eight points are stated:
first, contradiction with verbal expression;
second, contradiction with logical reasoning.
Third, contradiction regarding origination;
fourth, contradiction regarding coexistence;
fifth, contradiction regarding enmity.
The six obstacles and their remedies are mutually exclusive.
The five fruits are as explained in the separate chapter.
Since it has already been stated that the "functioning of man" (*puruṣakāra*) is included within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), [it refers to] the field, water, and so forth.
Therefore, we know that distinct dharmas are also termed "virile activity" (*puruṣakāra*).
Otherwise, indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas would lack this cause,
for all six kinds of bases are said to be indeterminate.
Since it is known that the basis for the activity of human effort (puruṣakāra) consists of the field, water, and so forth,
it is clearly understood that the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) is not obtained by the person alone; rather,
it is obtained through the immediately preceding cessation and the objective sphere (ālambana).
In the commentary (*śāstra*), there are three or four bases [for the arising of consciousness].

Why is it that true vision (*tattvadarśana*) lacks the "immediately preceding cessation" (*anantaranirodha*) among the two types of conformity? Answer: Because it fully encompasses the six and distinguishes the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. If that is so, then there would be two types of equal and immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).

Because the true grasping of views (*satya-dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) draws forth a subsequent pure state (*anāsrava*), it does not take that which has just ceased as its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-niruddha*).
This is because it conforms to the inferior [state] while drawing forth the intermediate one.

If the retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*) were to obtain [its cause] through the causes of projection (*ākṣepaka*), arising (*abhinirvartaka*), certainty (*niyata*), difference (*visabhāga*), and non-contradiction (*avirodhaka*), [then this would follow].
This explains that the ten causes of defiled phenomena obtain the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
If the ten causes are neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena,
they do not obtain this fruit, as determined by the Thirty-Eighth [Treatise].
That [unwholesome state] also functions as a cause for subsequent expression, a conditionally dependent cause, a cause of common activity, and a non-contradictory cause;
furthermore, it acts as a contradictory cause with respect to the indeterminate.
Among those ten causes for purification,
two causes yield the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*):
namely, the appropriating cause (*parigrahahetu*) and the opposing cause (*virodhahetu*).
The cause for the gathering of purification consists in:
approaching virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, attending to it with correct mental attention,
and practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, the perfection of the faculties (*indriya*) achieved through prior actions is called the "appropriating cause" (*parigraha-hetu*).
This indicates that it serves as the appropriating cause for supramundane phenomena;
therefore, one attains the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
Regarding contradictory causes:

if the various contradictory causes belonging to the category of purification are themselves the causes of afflicted phenomena, they thereby obtain the fruit of maturation (*vipāka*). Because of this commonality of function, those that are not contradictory also obtain the fruit of maturation.
Because it is the cause of appropriation,
there is no fault in the treatise’s reliance on the cause of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
Alternatively, neither of these [explanations] applies.
Because pure dharmas take pure dharmas as their cause,
they have no ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).
They do, however, obtain all three kinds of outflowing fruits (*niṣyandaphala*) through the ten causes.
Regarding the fact that the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is not said to be obtained through arising, causality,
and so forth: the second fascicle previously stated,
"The perfuming agent produces the seeds."
The seeds arise as actual manifestations,
just as the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) obtains the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala).
The seventh fascicle states:
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) produced in this life is called "of all kinds.
How is it that the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is said below to obtain the fruit of human effort? There are two interpretations.
One says: as in the Hīnayāna.
This is not accepted according to the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
Second, it is said that it may also be obtained as in that text;
here, it refers to the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) based on a distinct entity.
Because they do not share a composite nature, they are not contradictory.
The fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) is obtained only from pure causes and not from the other two [types of causes].
Why is it that defiled phenomena, being contrary to their causes, cannot obtain the fruit of disjunction?
The thirty-eighth [section] states:
It refers to being endowed with the supramundane lineage and encountering a Buddha’s appearance in the world to proclaim the True Dharma.
Associating with virtuous friends, hearing the true Dharma,
attending to it according to principle, practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma,
and all the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Because it is the cause that opposes these factors of affliction (*saṃkleśa*),
this [cause] is not said to yield the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
However, regarding the explanation of the cause of pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*), it is said:
If the various causes that are contrary to the category of affliction (saṃkleśa) are themselves the causes of pure phenomena (vyavadāna),
one should know that the causes contrary to affliction likewise attain the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyoga).
In this context, only the causes that accord with purification are discussed;

therefore, [the others] are omitted. Furthermore, because they are contrary causes to defilement, and because defiled phenomena are not the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*), [those contrary causes] cannot be established [as such].
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, chapter four, states: "What, then, is this?

It refers to the consciousness of the body, the consciousness of the owner of the body, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of that which is experienced, the consciousness of that which experiences, the consciousness of time, the consciousness of number, the consciousness of place, and the consciousness of verbal expression."
This [consciousness] arises from the seeds of the perfuming of conventional designations (*nāma-vyavahāra*).
As for the consciousness that distinguishes between self and others,
this arises from the seeds of the perfuming of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the consciousness of death and birth in the good and evil realms of existence,
this arises from the seeds perfumed by the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*);
by means of these various consciousnesses, all realms and destinies are comprised within the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
The dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) and false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*) are both manifested.
Among the three types of perfuming (*vāsanā*), these are distinguished by way of eight gates. First, the determination of their essential substance (*svabhāva*).
Second, the explanation of the names;
third, the establishment and abolition [of categories]. These should be reflected upon.
Fourth, regarding the three realms:
there is no contradiction in the existence of matter and sound that are the fruits of the formless realm concentrations.
Fifth, regarding the three natures.
Sixth, the eight consciousnesses;
seventh, the existence or non-existence of outflows;
eighth, the sequence of stages.

For what reason does the second fascicle state that the *pariṇāma* (transformations) consist only of *niṣyanda* (outflow) and *vipāka* (maturation), yet do not mention *ātmasaṃkleśa* (self-clinging)? Why is this mentioned here? [Furthermore,] regarding the establishment and exclusion of the twelve links [of dependent origination].
As stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*:
"Obscuration, establishment,
guidance, gathering, and fulfillment."
Because they are, respectively: discrimination, enjoyment, instigation, binding,
manifestation, suffering, and fruit.
Only this vexes the world:
the three, two, and seven defilements,
arising from false conceptualization.
The treatise states that since the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is that which is projected,
it is evident that the seeds of karma are subsumed under the projecting karma;
thus, as with consciousness, karma itself serves as the projector.
The seeds of consciousness are subsumed within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
They are encompassed by the three types and two types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Question: For what reason must ignorance (*avidyā*) be manifest at the time of initiating karma?
Regarding the stage of moistening karma (*karmopacaya*), it also includes that which is solely of the nature of seeds. Answer: Both principles are equal.
This is because, within the aforementioned non-negligence (*apramāda*), the merit of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and the immovable [merit] arise solely from seeds.
The Sūtra states that it is not ignorance (*avidyā*) that produces [the link].
If the seed also does not produce it,
how can it be called "not having clarity as its condition" and "not being contrary to the members of existence"?
In what way does this differ from [the case of] seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*)?

From this it is known that only the seeds (*bīja*) also produce [results]. Question: If that is so, why do the first members of the path (*pratipadāṅga*) when arising in higher realms not arise from seeds alone? Answer: Because manifest ignorance (*avidyā*) acts as the predominant cause for their arising.
Because they perceive the existence [of things] due to ignorance regarding the ultimate truth, they differ from ordinary beings who are not heedless.
As stated in [the *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*], fascicle 89: [text].
Regarding the "appropriation" (*upādāna*) branch, which consists of the grasper, the grasped, and that for which there is grasping:

when one who has been born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and fallen into the most grievous miserable destinies (*apāya*) perceives evil signs, they no longer give rise to longing; thus, the karma of the desire realm is light and does not lead [to rebirth].
Furthermore, those who die and are reborn in the two upper realms or in the evil destinies do not perceive the signs of the evil states;
they perceive the signs of their future fellow-beings.
Consequently, within that very life, there arises craving characterized by seeking;
because its origination does not rely on the previous meaning, it is said to be "unseeking.
This summarizes the meaning of all branches [of dependent origination] as being comprised of craving and views.

If it were not so, those born in the higher realms would not produce the lower miserable destinies, and craving and grasping would be non-existent, because they would find no pleasure in either the present or the future.
In this context, "provisional" (prajñapti) refers to that which appropriates other factors as its own identity; thus it is called "provisional."
It is not the case that something is called "provisional" (prajñapti) simply because it does not grasp another thing as its own essence;

nor is it said to be provisional because it lacks intrinsic substance and function within its own constituents. This is because within conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), there are things called "provisional," such as names (nāman) and so forth, which are themselves of the nature of form (rūpa).
To claim that consciousness consists of only a single entity contradicts the ninth yoga;
for that [text] takes the six consciousnesses as its basis.
Therefore, the *Ninji-san* (The Ninety-three) states:
"That [treatise] takes all continuities as its subject of discussion;
it does not concern the actual physical body."
Because this is spoken of as real,
that which is to be abandoned is explained in fifty-nine [places].
Afflictions can be abandoned by means of their associated factors and their objects.
Why is this? Because when the path of antidote arises, afflictions do not occur, and one attains the state of non-arising dharmas.
Therefore, it is said that they are "severed from their association.
Once the association is severed, they no longer take objects as conditions;
thus, they are also said to be "severed" with respect to their objects. However, the *Ṣaṭpañcāśatka* states:
The existence of outflows (āsrava) is established by way of five aspects:
first, by way of the object;
second, by way of the latent dispositions (anuśaya).
1) Because of their association;
2) because of their object;
3) because of their arising.
What is the objective basis of tainted phenomena?
It refers to internal pure form,
as well as external form— both that which is dependent upon it and that which is not dependent upon it.
Whether they be defiled minds and mental factors, or wholesome or neutral minds and mental factors—
these contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) are designated as "contaminated" by way of the other four characteristics, as appropriate to each case.
That is to say, by virtue of being latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth:
if the seeds of affliction have not been harmed or severed within pure forms, as well as within all minds and mental factors as previously described, they are termed "latent dispositions."
It is also called "gross heaviness" (dauṣṭhulya).
