One should know that as long as these have not been abandoned without remainder, all things are called "with outflows" (sāsrava) by virtue of the underlying tendencies (anuśaya). This is the intended meaning here.
Regarding pure forms, when they are associated with defiled, wholesome, or neutral minds and mental factors,
because the seeds of all afflictions have not yet been harmed or abandoned,
these very seeds are called *anuśaya* (latent tendencies).
It is also called "dysfunction" (dausthulya).
Therefore, based on these latent dispositions (anuśaya), they are designated as "with outflows" (sāsrava) within this category of mental factors (caitta).

If defiled minds and mental factors are said to be "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) by virtue of association, it is because they coexist with them; this applies to all things that possess a basis and all objects within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Whatever arises through the predominance of that which is produced by the outflows—because all such things have the outflows as their object—they are called "with outflows. In this context, the present is termed "possessing a basis" (savastuka).

The past and the future are called "non-existent entities. Within the present, that which is traversed by consciousness based on pure form is called "the range of direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*). This refers to the five objects of the five sensory consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manas*) that arises simultaneously with them.

That which is the domain of direct perception is called "the domain of direct perception"; that which is the domain of anything else is called "not the domain of direct perception. Furthermore, all external sense bases arise with the internal sense bases as their dominant condition.

They are termed "arisen from the predominance of that which is with outflows" (sāsrava), referring to the external bases (bāhyāyatana) transformed by the eighth consciousness and others; or, although they are objects of direct perception (pratyakṣa), they constitute "with outflows" because they are not [proper] objects of cognition (ālambana).
This refers to all objects of the concentrated mind and so forth.
Therefore, it is further stated in the third instance that they are "arisen from the predominance produced by the out-flowing [of karma].
These exist only as the five sensory objects (pañca-viṣaya) perceived by the five, sixth, and eighth consciousnesses; one should know that those very objects of perception are out-flowing (sāsrava).
Why is this? If various afflictions were to arise by taking the past and future as their objects,
[they could not do so] because the past and future lack any substantial entity.
It is not on account of its object that it is called "with outflows" (sāsrava).
For instance, present things that are not within the range of direct perception (pratyakṣa),
such as pure matter (rūpa) and all defiled, wholesome, or neutral minds and mental factors (citta-caitta).
Those [dharmas] are not called "outflowing" (*sāsrava*) because they are the objects of the afflictions;
rather, the various afflictions arise from the marks produced by one's own conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

This is because those dharmas do not serve as the distinct objective domains for such [afflictions]. Based on this, there are only five objects, consisting of both the primary substance and its reflected image in the present.

That which is designated as "having outflows" (sāsrava) by virtue of its object is everything else. That which becomes "having outflows" by virtue of its arising refers to those cases where the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) have not been permanently abandoned.
Because the objects conducive to the afflictions appear before one,
and because improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) arises toward them;
by these causes and conditions, all phenomena [are produced].
Whether currently arising, already arisen, or yet to arise—
all such things are called "with outflows" (sāsrava) because they originate from them.
Furthermore, [they arise] from all unwholesome afflictions (kleśa).
All resultant fruits (*vipākaphala*), as well as the external phenomena produced by the predominance of resultant fruits—
all such things arise as well; therefore,
they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
This is explained at length up to the characteristics of the arising of outflows (*āsrava*).
That which is currently arising is accompanied by outflows;
that which is about to arise is what brings them forth.
Those that have already arisen arise intermittently;
together with their associated and object-corresponding factors, there are five types of conjunctions.
This explains the case of the tainted (sāsrava).
Although there are five distinct characteristics,
when discussing the gate of abandonment, the primary antidotes for abandonment do not exceed two types.
Both the direct and the indirect are bonds of the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Therefore, the treatise states that there are no more than two types of abandonment.
Now, it is explained that there are distinctions in meaning based on differences in directness and indirectness;
thus, there are variations such as that which is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If it were not so, the seventh [consciousness] taking the eighth as its object would not be called "hidden" (*saṃvṛta*),
because it is said that when the perceiving subject is severed, the perceived object is also severed.

Therefore, one should understand it exactly as explained herein. Furthermore, while the principle of the sequential progression of those two types of abandonment has been interpreted, here we speak according to the actual meaning:
that which is *sāsrava* (contaminated) possesses five characteristics. Nevertheless, all contaminated phenomena can be summarized into five categories.
The five external objects beyond the first dhyāna are called "with outflows" (sāsrava) solely by virtue of being bound by a single object of perception;
because they do not reside within [the mind], they are not associated with the outflows.
The five faculties of the second happy realm (sugati) are internal objects;
they become contaminated (sāsrava) by two factors:
namely, their objects of perception (ālambana) and their association with outflows (āsrava).
Because they are internal,
the external objects of those unwholesome karmas are also twofold:
first, the object of perception (ālambana).
Second, they are drawn by the outflows (*āsrava*).
Third, with the exception of the results of the miserable destinies (*apāya*),
the remaining unobscured-neutral minds and mental factors arise due to three conditions.
First, having the same object of focus, such as the seventh condition being related to the eighth and so forth;
second, being accompanied by outflows (*āsrava*);
third, arising with an interval.

Within the miserable destinies, the five faculties and the four objects also arise from three conditions: namely, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the condition of being associated with outflows (*āsrava-sahabhū*), and the condition of being drawn forth by outflows (*āsrava-ākṣepa*).
The fourth [category], the wholesome mind and mental factors, arise from four conditions.
That is to say: having an object of perception, being accompanied by outflows (*āsrava*), arising intermittently, and being induced by outflows.

The unobscured-neutral minds and mental factors that result in rebirth in the evil destinies likewise have these four [characteristics], because they are induced by the unwholesome and the tainted (*sāsrava*).
Fifth, all defiled minds and mental factors arise due to five conditions:

namely, the object-condition (*ālambana*), coexistence with outflows (*āsrava-sahabhū*), immediate succession (*antara-janman*), being drawn forth by outflows (*āsrava-ākṣepa*), and association (*samprayoga*). Regarding association, the Mahāyāna differs from the Hīnayāna in its two types of objects.
The essence of the outflows consists of the afflictions and their secondary afflictions;
the eight consciousnesses, the universal, the object-specific, and the indeterminate mental factors— these four categories—
are by nature neutral (avyākṛta).
That which is associated with the eleven wholesome [mental factors] is called wholesome.
When that mind and its mental factors are accompanied by afflictions and secondary afflictions, they are called defiled mind and mental factors.
Those afflictions and secondary afflictions are dharmas whose nature is to be abandoned.
That which is associated with consciousness and so forth is termed "abandoned through dissociation" (*visaṃyoga-prahāṇa*);
that is, all defiled minds and mental factors are abandoned through dissociation.
Other non-defiled phenomena are abandoned through the abandonment of their objects (*ālambana-prahāṇa*).
Because the remote object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) pervades all that exists,
the "intrinsic nature that is abandoned" mentioned in the treatise refers specifically to the defiled mind and its mental factors.
Those afflictions that are dissociated from their objects consist of both direct and indirect objects;
those afflictions that are associated with them involve those same objects.
This refers to the three types of intermixture: innate intermixture (*sahaja-saṃkīrṇa*), induced intermixture (*ākṣepaka-saṃkīrṇa*), and intermittent intermixture (*vyavakīrṇa*).
Based on these, one should distinguish that the eighth consciousness can take both [the defiled and the pure] as its objects within the happy realms.
First, those with a single object;
second, those associated with outflows; third, those pertaining to the miserable destinies. There are three [types] of the latter.
Furthermore, it induces the eighth [consciousness] to manifest its objective aspect (nimittabhāga);
this is likewise the case for the good and evil destinies.
However, the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of all seeds possess their respective meanings according to the various manifesting conceptualizations (*vikalpa*);
external objects do not do so.
The seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the seventh consciousness has five conditions:
first, association (*samprayoga*);
second, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Third, it gives rise to [the next life]; fourth, it arises in the interval;
fifth, it is associated with outflows (*āsrava*), because it is defiled.
The image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is common to both the sentient and the non-sentient,
because it possesses the nature of both; it has only an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), is associated with outflows (sāsrava), and is also induced by outflows.
Because the image exists within the mind and because it is induced by defiled views, the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the sixth consciousness permeates all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*),
just as was explained regarding the three natures of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Among the indeterminate [states], the two minds of deportment and craftsmanship arise through three [conditions]:
namely, by way of arising in succession, by way of co-arising, and by way of the object-condition (*ālambana*).
Herein, the object-condition functions as the seed-condition (*bīja-pratyaya*).
Even that which is currently active cannot be called an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
The past and future lack substantial existence,
and in the present, there is necessarily no defiled mind that takes them as its object.
The rest are all to be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the maturation mind (*vipākacitta*), it arises from four [causes];
among these three [types of causes], the outflowing cause (*āsravāvedhaka*) is added.
The resultant indeterminate mind and its mental factors arise from two conditions:
first, the object-condition;
second, the condition of association with outflows.
A wholesome mind and its mental factors arise from four causes:
namely, those associated with outflows, those arising from immediate succession, those that are projected, and those that are objective conditions.
Defiled states arise from five causes.

Among its objective aspects (*nimittabhāga*), all those conditioned by different realms, those conditioned by the untainted (*anāsrava*), and those lacking a real basis (*nirālambana*) are termed "sole images" (*kevalapratibimba*).
This is explained according to the nature of the subjective cognition (*ālambaka*), with the exception of the associated factors (*samprayukta*).
The good destinies (*sugati*) possess five faculties as their essential nature and are exclusively dependent on them; furthermore, the internal five objects and so forth arise from two conditions:
namely, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the outflow-condition (*āsrava-sahabhū*).
The external fruits of the evil destinies (*durgati*) likewise possess these two.
That is to say, the objects of focus (ālambana) and the outflows (āsrava).
Furthermore, the internal faculties (indriya) and objects (viṣaya) within the miserable destinies (apāya) arise from two causes;
that is to say, the objects of focus and the outflows.

All are the same as the preceding sense-gate [discussions]. The seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the five consciousnesses also pervades the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), all being the same as the sixth [consciousness].
The image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) in the happy realms is exclusively the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Internally, they are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*);
for the evil destinies, add "drawn by outflows.
Although there are such cases, the outflows are not identical.
It is merely through the predominance of the two fetters— conjunction (*samprayoga*) and object (*ālambana*)— that the two types of abandonment are established;
it is not by relying on names such as "abandonment of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*) and so forth,
as was analyzed previously in the seventh consciousness and the sixth consciousness proofs.
Regarding the three types of suffering, if one relies on the characteristic of the suffering of birth:
the first two pertain only to the desire realm,
while the last one pervades all three realms.
If one considers their nature, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) pertains only to the desire realm because of the presence of oppressive conditions;
the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) extends throughout the form realm.
Because there is the experience of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
As it is said in the Sūtra, one enters a mind that undergoes transformation;
the latter [category] pervades all three realms.
Since the six factors— consciousness and the rest— within the state of being accompanied by the three feelings are seeds,
how do they correspond?
There are two interpretations for this.
First, it is explained according to the state of being about to arise;
second, it is explained according to the sense of conformity with the co-existent [factors].
Thus, there is no contradiction.

Therefore, the term "seed" (bīja) is called "concomitant" (sahabhū). Since "concomitant" is a synonym for "associated" (saṃprayukta), if that is so, how can there be association when the seeds of the future existence-constituents (bhava-aṅga) have not yet arisen?
[The answer is: The five types, beginning with consciousness (vijñāna), are said to be associated because their seeds exist as actualities (samudācāra) within the future existence.

Because the power of the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) has previously been associated with the factors of volitional formations (*saṃskārāṅga*) and so forth, the seeds are also said to be associated;
alternatively, this is stated from the perspective of the stage when consciousness and the subsequent factors are about to arise.
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* explains the essence of the four truths, such as suffering,
as in the commentary.
In the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*, it is explained within the context of the twelvefold reverse contemplation.
The birth-factors and the five beginning with consciousness are all the accumulation of old age and death; thus,
their nature as suffering and accumulation is identical.
There are two kinds of "origination" (*samudaya*):
first, that which brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) is called origination;
this is what is explained in the *Viniścaya*.
Only karma and afflictions—
these two that can produce the fruit of suffering— are called the "Origin" (samudaya).
This refers to the factors such as the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) discussed in the "Chapter on the Compendium of Bases" (*Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*).
Although these two treatises differ, they are not mutually contradictory.
The two types of birth-and-death are distinguished by means of eight gates.
First, the essential nature;
second, the explanation of the name;
third, the discernment of the distinct characteristics of the production of birth and death.
Fourth, the explanation of the stages and positions.
Fifth, the explanation of the locus of attainment.
Sixth, the mutual inclusion of the four kinds of birth-and-death.
Seventh, the three types of *saṃsāra* differ across the seven assemblies.

Eighth, the analysis through questions and answers. Regarding these three gates—essence (*tattva*), name (*nāman*), and questions and answers—they are as explained in the treatise. The locus of their attainment is as previously stated in the seventh fascicle, in the explanation of the arising of the untainted (*anāsrava*) within the eighth consciousness.
However, one should carefully distinguish the differences among the various fruits.
Regarding their sequence, those such as the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and others attain [the first fruit] upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*),
as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścaya*, the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, and the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding the differences among these three types of birth and death,
as cited in the commentary from the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*,
they are nonetheless determined according to the three vehicles based on the three bodies (*trikāya*) in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and this treatise.
The *Laṅkāvatāra* is taught solely for those who rely on the Mahāyāna and attain sudden awakening, being terrified of the afflictions;
alternatively, it may be said to generally address those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*) in their distinguished stages,
wherein the period of one kalpa prior to the [first] bhūmi is no different from the original state.

The reason why the distinct characteristics of birth and death produced by discrimination are not explained here is that there are two types of *paricchinna* (segmented existence): first, the scattered;
second, the continuous.
Second, regarding concentration. Within the state of distraction, there are two types:
first, that which arises according to the twelve links of dependent origination.
It exists only in the entirety of the desire realm and in a small portion of the higher realms;
it is distinguished by its retribution based on the innate wholesome [roots].
Second, based on superior hearing and reflection, there arises the wholesome mind obtained through birth (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala-citta*).
The various material requisites that give rise to the prolongation of merit, longevity, and fortune exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because the mind therein is sharp and intense.
Within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are three types.
First, there is the practice of transferring merit and longevity through a contaminated meditative absorption (*sāsrava-samādhi*),
which exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Second, there is birth in the Heaven of Vast Results (*brhatphala*) within the four dhyānas, as well as in the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Only tainted karma perfumes the three grades of dhyāna that give rise to birth in the five Pure Abodes;
these births are a mixture of the untainted and the transformed. The transformed body (nirmāṇakāya) consists of only two types:
first, that which is produced by tainted vows and so forth, and second, that which is entirely untainted.
They are supported by their former karma;
that is to say, all those of the two vehicles prior to the seventh stage have already been supported by the active manifestation of ignorance and other factors as conditions.
Second, from the eighth stage upward,
there are only uncontaminated meditative concentrations as their provisions,
because the active cognitive obstructions and so forth have all been eliminated. Regarding the inclusion of the four types of birth and death:
The *Anuttara-sūtra* states:
"Ānanda, all arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the ten stages,
due to four kinds of hindrances, are unable to attain the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya and the pāramitās of the four virtues."
What are the four? First, the condition for arising;
second, the cause for arising.
Third is existence; fourth is non-existence.
What is the condition for birth? It is the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), which is able to produce all formative activities (*saṃskāra*).
Just as ignorance gives rise to karma,
what is the cause for the arising of afflictions?
These are the various formations produced by the ground of the dwelling of ignorance.
For example, just as various karmas arise from ignorance,
what constitutes "existence" (bhava) that is conditioned by the ground of the abiding of ignorance?
The three kinds of mind-made bodies arise from outflow-free formations produced by the ground of the abiding of ignorance, just as,
for example, the four types of grasping serve as conditions.
With the three outflows (āsrava) as causes for karma,
the three kinds of existence (bhava) arise. What is non-existence?
Based on the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*),
there is a subtle passing away that cannot be perceived, just as,
based on the three realms of existence (*bhava*), there is moment-to-moment aging and death. As it says further below:
Ānanda, within the three realms there are four kinds of difficulties:
first, the difficulty of afflictions;
second, the difficulty of karma.
Third is the difficulty of birth-retribution;
fourth is the difficulty of faults:
the *upāya-bhava* (birth through expedient means) arising from the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).
The afflictions within the triple world are difficult to overcome;
the birth and death arising from the causal conditions of the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) are like the karmic difficulties within the triple world.
The existence and non-existence of birth and death arising from the ground of the abiding of ignorance are like the difficulty of producing roots within the three realms.
Birth and death arising from the ground of the abiding of ignorance do not exist.
As it is difficult to find faults within the three realms:
those who possess existence have the retributive essence of the three realms,
while those who lack existence are free from the suffering of suffering and the other forms of suffering.

There is only the characteristic of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Even that which is supported by the untainted (*anāsrava*) is said to be difficult, as distinguished in the dialogue.
Having attained the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), one passes through three great eons.
Is it also possible to undergo transformation and attain the rhinoceros-like [solitary buddha] state for a hundred kalpas? Answer: No, it is not possible.
This is because one does not take the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as a condition; rather, the retained body is sustained by the support of tainted meditative concentration and vows.

Regarding the inclusion within the *paricchinna-kāya* (segmented body): even if one were to grant that it is produced by the assistance of untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) and vows (*praṇidhāna*), what fault would there be in not admitting this?
Because it is supremely excellent, it is not subsumed under the category of the segmented body.
Those who are not subject to transformation cannot maintain their bodies for a long duration without outflows (*anāsrava*),
because their power is weak.
The Abhidharma states fourteen types of discrimination.

That is to say: discrimination of non-existence, discrimination of existence, discrimination of superimposition, discrimination of denial, discrimination of identity, discrimination of difference, discrimination of intrinsic nature, discrimination of specific distinction, discrimination of the object according to the name, and discrimination of the name according to the object.
This is explained in detail according to the corresponding passages in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
which establishes the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) through their preceding, succeeding,
and intermediate sections; this differs from the three versions found in other locations.
As reconciled in the *Vijñaptimātra* chapter: why is it that the principle of the two emptinesses has degrees of depth?
One need not realize the [emptiness of] persons in order to realize phenomena;
yet regarding the two natures, when one does not realize the deeper level, one necessarily does not realize the shallower level.

To penetrate the principle is precisely to penetrate the phenomena. The answer is twofold: first, the obstacle of the distinction between principle and phenomena, which prevents one from severing the grasping at birth and awakening to the emptiness of dharmas;
second, the obstacle of the non-distinction between the two natures.
If one does not awaken to the fundamental [nature], one cannot awaken to derivative phenomena.
This is because there has never been a case where one first awakens to phenomena and only later awakens to the emptiness of birth;
one must first realize ultimate truth before comprehending conventional matters—this can be understood through reflection.
The three gates of liberation differ from the practices subsumed in various treatises;
these should be recorded separately. [They concern] the absence of intrinsic nature and impermanence.
In the Abhidharma and other treatises, all contemplations on the aspect of impermanence within the Truth of Suffering include this practice;
first, one eliminates what is grasped as real,
and subsequently, one contemplates the dependent nature.
Furthermore, both nature (*svabhāva*) and truth (*satya*) are real;
the phenomena that are the objects of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) are merely designated based on the dependent (*paratantra*). Is this solely for the sake of protecting the Dharma?
Is it also Sthiramati?
Regarding the texts of these two masters,
Dharmapāla personally adopted the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect).
An-hui maintains that all three natures are attained;
the three interpretations all attain them.
Examine this.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"In this way, because the bodhisattva realizes that mental discourse appears as the semblance of objects, he realizes the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
because he realizes it is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), he realizes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)."
If one has already eliminated the characteristics of consciousness-only that consist of the seeds of the mental verbalization of hearing the Dharma,
until such time as the Bodhisattva’s perfectly equal non-conceptual wisdom has arisen.
One realizes and enters into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, it is said:
"Names and things are mutually adventitious."
Its nature should be investigated;
regarding these two, one should also deduce that they are merely measure and merely conventional.
Through the wisdom of reality, one observes the absence of objects.
There are only three types of conceptual construction;
because that [object] does not exist, this [construction] does not exist.
This is precisely the entry into the three natures.
The first half-verse pertains to the realization of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
the subsequent half-verse pertains to the realization of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
and the final verse pertains to the realization of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

The *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states: "It is not the case that one can understand that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like illusory things and so forth—
existing yet not real— without having seen True Suchness (*tathatā*)."
Thus, there are three different levels above and below.
According to the initial passage of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the two stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Peak (*mūrdhan*) involve the entry into the grasped (*parikalpita*),
while Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) involve the entry into the dependent (*paratantra*).
At the initial mind of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), one enters the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
According to the second section of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, through the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), one investigates and realizes the first two natures;
through the four types of "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), one realizes the perfected nature.
In the *Cheng weishi lun wen yao*, one must enter the first stage (*bhūmi*) to realize the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Although there are three textual passages, their underlying principles are only two:
the first is twofold proof.
Second is "similarity.
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this refers to actual direct realization;
for it is only through the two untainted wisdoms (*anāsrava-jñāna*)—the wisdom of suchness and the wisdom of phenomena—that one can successively realize the latter two natures.
When realizing the two natures, one does not perceive the two types of grasping;
this is precisely what is meant by realizing the non-existence of that which is conceptually imputed. It is not that there is no ontological essence whatsoever.
What is realized by wisdom?
That which is the transformation of the mind is not subsumed under the dependent nature;
the principle of suchness is not subsumed under the perfected nature.
Therefore, regarding the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), no separate proof is stated;
rather, when one does not perceive the two types of grasping within the two natures,
this may be called "awakening into" the imagined nature.
However, the wisdom of the true essence (samyaktva-jñāna) realizes the principle that there is nothing to be realized;

it is commonly said that this wisdom realizes [the non-existence of] what is conceptually imputed (parikalpita). Although one has already not seen [these objects] even prior to the path of vision (darśana-mārga), [it is here that they are definitively realized as such].
Since one who has not yet personally attained these two is not said to have realized them, it is only at the first stage that they are called "attainment.
The opening passage of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that "realizing the perfected nature" refers to actual realization.
This is the same as in the case of *vijñaptimātra*.
The realization of the first two natures is based on a realization by way of similarity,
because for a long time one has predominantly engaged in conceptual reflection (*manasikāra*) through intellectual understanding (*adhimukti*) regarding those two natures.
Although there may be a similar realization of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) for a brief duration and on a small scale,
it is neither sustained over a long period nor extensive, nor is it a direct realization; therefore,
this is stated according to the actual reality.
The subsequent passage in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* concerning the realization of the three natures (trisvabhāva) is stated based on a general, analogous intention.
It is called "realizing the grasped" because one first observes that names and things are not inherently connected.
Next, one contemplates that all phenomena— such as the mere measure of consciousness and conventional designations—
are, although not yet realized as such,
the stage of the wisdom that understands the dependent nature as it truly is; for while its characteristics exist substantially, true reality has not yet been realized.
When both types of grasping have ceased, one enters into a state that resembles the true contemplation of reality;
even at the stage of intellectual understanding, it is considered to be suchness itself.
Therefore, the stage of actual wisdom is called "entry into the perfected nature" (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
In reality, one has not yet attained realization.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains the entry into realization by distinguishing the three natures based on a semblance of intellectual understanding (*adhimukti*),
whereas the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* bases its explanation on the actual, distinct realization of the two natures.
The scriptural citations proving [the existence of] the grasped, though their wording differs, are not contradictory;
all other passages should be interpreted accordingly.
The fifth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains eight similes as metaphors for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
When one conceptualizes what is non-existent,
why does it appear clearly as if it were an actual object of engagement?
To dispel this doubt, the analogy of a magical illusion is taught.
Just as there is no actual elephant but only an illusory elephant,

so too is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) regarding its objective sphere: although the six sense bases that take form and other objects as their spheres do not exist [in reality], they nevertheless appear.

When one engages in conceptual construction (*parikalpa*), there is an appearance of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as if they were objects of perception. Regarding this, the author himself explains below that "this gives rise to doubt concerning internal phenomena. Other masters explain it as follows:

Because doubt arises regarding the internal body, forms, sounds, smells, and so forth, the analogy of a magical illusion is taught. Master Vasubandhu provides two successive explanations; the second interpretation states:
In this context, the analogy of an illusion is used to eliminate [the misconception regarding] the six internal bases, such as the eye and so forth.
For example, although illusory forms do not exist in reality, they are perceived as appearing;
by this standard, one should understand the six bases, such as form and so forth, which lack intrinsic nature and serve as objects of perception.
It is not the six sense bases of form, sound, smell, and so forth;
rather, it refers to the phenomena of the six internal sense bases, such as the eye.
Because the eye and the others are material forms, they are described as "form" and so on.
It is not problematic to say that the six bases, such as visible form (*rūpa*), are also [included].
Otherwise, what difference would there be from the second category of what is excluded? An ancient interpretation states:
"The first refers to the substance of the object (*viṣaya*)."
The second is the receptacle world;

thus, there is a distinction between these two. Furthermore, just as when a mirage flickers, there is actually no water, yet there is the perception of water, so too is it with the external receptacle world.
Moreover, just as in a dream, the collection of mind and mental factors arising from sleep is extremely dull and obscure.
Although there are no objects such as women or various other things, there is still the experience of pleasant and unpleasant objects;
it is the same during the waking state. Furthermore, it is like seeing the original object reflected back within a mirror or similar surface.
Yet one thinks, "I now see a distinct reflection," whereas this reflection is actually non-existent;
it does not have the substantial nature of wholesome or unwholesome volitional karma from a state that is not in meditative equipoise as its objective condition.
The arising of the fruit as a reflection is likewise so.

Regarding "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra), it is like a mirror-image. Furthermore, it is like light and shadow: by one who plays with shadows, the light is obscured by a veil, and various shadows arise.
The various consciousnesses within the stages of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) evolve with respect to distinctions that lack any real objective basis. Furthermore,
just as an echo has no actual sound yet causes a listener to perceive it as a variety of spoken words and objects, so too do these consciousnesses appear.

Various verbal activities of speech are likewise so. Furthermore, it is like the moon in water: because of the water's moist, smooth, and clear nature, although there is no actual moon, the moon can be apprehended.
The mental factor associated with all samādhis is likewise characterized by being perfumed, cultivated, moistened, and purified by taking the object of the true meaning as its condition.
Although there is no objective realm of real meaning as an object of focus, it appears to function as if it existed.
What is the difference between this and the fourth [type of] image?

There is a distinction based on whether one is in a state of meditative concentration or a non-concentrated state. Furthermore, it is like a magical creation which, depending upon this [basis], is called a "magical creation."
Although there is no reality,
the one who performs the transformation is free from error and exerts diligent effort toward the task of transforming others.
The Bodhisattva is likewise:
although there are no sentient beings that are conceptually imputed,
[he acts] toward all classes of sentient beings within the dependent nature.
Out of compassion, he goes to those various places of rebirth to assume a physical body. Wuxing’s commentary states:
"One should know that within this there is a metaphor for such matters of false attachment."
This refers to the distinctions between internal and external enjoyments;
bodily actions, vocal actions, and the three types of mental actions—whether in a state of non-equipoise or in a state of equipoise—that are free from error.
Regarding these eight matters,
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught eight similes for the sake of those who possess wisdom.
Having heard what was thus spoken, one is able to correctly understand the meaning of the two stages:
the determinate and the indeterminate. Herein, "internal" refers to—
The first is manifested by the analogy of magical illusions;
the second, external [world], is manifested by the analogy of a mirage;
these constitute the distinctions in enjoyment.
This refers to bodily action (kāyakarman), which is illustrated by the third simile of the dream; it refers to [bodily action],
which is illustrated by the fifth simile of the reflected image.
Vocal action is illustrated by the sixth simile, that of an echo.
Among the three types of mental action, the first pertains to a state that is not in meditative equipoise (*asamāhita-bhūmi*).
This is illustrated by the fourth analogy of the reflection;
that which belongs to the stage of meditative equipoise is illustrated by the seventh analogy of the moon in water.
If there is no inversion,
this is what is revealed by the eighth simile of transformation. Regarding Vasubandhu Bodhisattva’s two successive expositions,
the second exposition states:
The analogy of magical illusions is taught to eliminate [clinging to] the six internal sense bases, such as the eye; the analogy of a mirage is taught [to eliminate clinging to the external objects].
To eliminate [the misconception of] the receptacle world,
the metaphor of a dream is taught;
to eliminate [the misconception of] the objects of enjoyment, such as form and so forth.
It demonstrates that forms and so forth, which are like dreams, are definitely non-existent,
yet they can act as causes for the arising of distinctions in the experience of pleasant and unpleasant sensations;
the simile of a reflected image is taught to eliminate [the misconception regarding] the fruit of bodily action.
It is taught that, with wholesome and unwholesome karma as conditions,
other forms arise as reflected images;
this is explained by the analogy of an echo.
To eliminate misconceptions regarding the fruit of vocal karma,
it is taught that the cause of vocal karma produces its fruit like an echo; thus,
the analogy of light and shadow is given.
This is to exclude the fruits of mental karma belonging to the non-concentrated stages (*asamāhita-bhūmi*),
thereby demonstrating that the various fruits obtained from this mental karma are like reflections and shadows.
The analogy of the moon in water is taught to eliminate [the misconception regarding] the fruits of mental karma belonging to the meditative equipoise stage,
demonstrating that the fruits of mental karma belonging to the meditative equipoise stage are just like the moon in water.
The analogy of transformation is taught in order to eliminate mental karma of the type consisting of hearing.
That which consists of hearing refers to what has been perfumed by hearing and reflection.
This demonstrates that the mental faculty (manas) functions by way of distinctions in the types of what has been heard,
like a magical transformation.
This mental faculty serves to eliminate the distinctions in internal and external enjoyments, as well as the three types of mental karma resulting from bodily and vocal actions.
Therefore, eight similes are taught to show that [the nature of phenomena] is not the same as non-existence. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states:
"All conditioned phenomena..."
One should contemplate [the body] as being like a star, a cataract, a lamp, a magical illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud.
These are the nine similes herein.
The Bodhisattva Devaśarman’s commentary states:
"There are nine distinct metaphors, namely:
seeing, characteristics, consciousness, the vessel-world, the body, sensation, the past, the present, and the future world; therefore, nine metaphors are taught."
Each [explanation] relies on a distinct meaning and cannot be harmonized,
because the commentaries on the verses differ. The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* explains eight metaphors.
It applies generally to both the dependent nature and the imagined nature;
it is like the dependent nature in appearance,
but like the imagined nature in reality.
Nor is there any contradiction.
Among the objects of the three natures for both ordinary beings and sages, there are four preceding passages; when combined with what should be stated as the actual teaching, there are five in total.
One should reflect according to reason.
One should establish three types of designations in total;
that is, one should establish one as real and one as a designation.
Because *tathatā* (suchness) is the true, ultimate reality,
as stated in the one hundredth fascicle;
all else is conventional and provisional.
Alternatively, there are those that do not depend on these others and are real, such as form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth;
those that depend on these others and are conventional, such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth;
or those that are real without depending on verbal designations (*nāman*).
That is to say, all phenomena depend upon names and expressions as mere designations;
that is to say, all phenomena.
As explained in the commentary on the third fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 60) regarding karma and the paths of action (*karmapatha*) and so forth contradicts the first fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Examine this: In the ninth fascicle, regarding the question of how foolish people superimpose false attachments upon those [dharmas],
it is also stated that there are wrong views that deny their existence.
Why is it said that there is only superimposition (*samāropa*)? Answer: Because it occurs for the most part;
for the conceptualization of a self and phenomena necessarily involves superimposition.
It is taught that there are three natures (*trisvabhāva*) in order to exclude the door of denial (*apavāda*).
The teaching on the three natures serves as a door for negating superimposition (*samāropa*).
Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it lacks spontaneous arising;
for there are two kinds of spontaneity.
First, arising spontaneously without a cause;
this encompasses all [views of] causelessness.
Second, arising with spontaneity as the cause.
By citing this, all [theories] involving a cause that is either non-equal to its nature (*asama-svabhāva*) or not so,

as well as those asserting causelessness (*ahetu*) or spontaneous occurrence (*svabhāva*), are subsumed; for there is no such thing as causeless spontaneity, nor is there anything that arises spontaneously from a non-equal cause.
Therefore, it is called "spontaneous non-arising. Within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), there are likewise various instances of causelessness and improper causes;
why, then, is only spontaneous arising negated? Answer: For the time being, spontaneous arising is cited as the primary example.
All other causes of inequality are subsumed under these;
this teaching of the three natures of non-existence refutes [the view of] superimposition,
whereas other forms of denial contradict the three natures.
Therefore, this does not refute the absence of causes.
The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is called "ultimate non-nature" (paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā).
Although the treatise merely uses the term "non-" (niḥ-), it is not that the ultimate nature itself is called "ultimate non-nature."

Furthermore, there is that which has an essence that is ultimately non-existent, yet is designated as "ultimately non-existent" because it is an object of the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
As it is said, these are subsumed within those four types of ultimate reality.
The treatise omits them briefly,
yet they exist logically as well;
within the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only), there are only two pairs.
Why are the former two not described as being false?
Because uncontaminated conditioned phenomena are not false.
Why are the former two not described as the conventional in contrast to the ultimate?
As it is said regarding the two ultimate truths,
the former is also called conventional; therefore, here, based on the presence of substantiality, it is termed "conventional," whereas that [other] lacks substantiality.
In reality, it also exists,
according to the two truths. Herein,
"real nature" refers exclusively to *tathatā* (suchness).
There are only the gates of permanence and impermanence;
the gates of the outflowing and the non-outflowing are not taught because conditioned phenomena that are non-outflowing lack a real intrinsic nature.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains that the cultivation of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā) occurs in four stages,

There is also a remote potentiality.
Furthermore, the seeds of delusion persist for a long duration during the state of transformation,
without depending on the accumulation of numerical factors.
If there were no seeds of affliction, the period of transformation would be brief;

as with those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning, they must repeatedly rely on the power of vows. However, there are four permutations: there are cases where only meditative concentration is superior and lacks the assistance of the seeds of affliction.
Nor do they undergo transformation for a long duration,
as in the case of those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning and turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna],
even though they possess the assistance of the seeds of afflictions.
They lack the provisions for supreme meditative concentration,
nor do they persist for a long duration,
as is the case with those of the two vehicles who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] while still in the stage of training.
Those who possess the assistance of afflictions and the resources of superior meditative concentration undergo transformation and experience [rebirth] for a long duration,
such as the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
Therefore, I wish to retain it.
This is not a matter of retaining it because its cessation is improper— as is the case with the Two Vehicles, who sever it—
nor is it merely a matter of planting auxiliary seeds as the Two Vehicles do.
It is not that it is not designated as "retained" because it lacks the support of aspiration;
rather, the bodhisattva relies primarily on the support of aspiration and secondarily on the assistance of the seeds.
Therefore, it is said that they are retained.
If one were to sever them immediately, they would lack the power to produce [further results],
because once the cause of delusion is extinguished, its effects follow suit in being exhausted.
Furthermore, because a bodhisattva’s intention, the stages of enlightenment (*bodhi-bhūmi*), and the refinement of the faculties do not require the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*),
and because the presence of these afflictions does not obstruct the attainment of the stages, they are termed "retained."
The path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) abandons [the afflictions] instantaneously. The fifty-nine moments of the three minds are also called "instantaneous.
However, the two obstacles—the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*)—are each divided into two. What are these two?
If one were to first eliminate the coarse categories by means of the nine grades,
then the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) should likewise first eliminate the coarse. If,
however, one distinguishes between the coarse and the subtle based on what obstructs the path, [then the distinction is as follows].
The ninth stage is indeterminate.
Regarding the "Chapter on Afflictions," how can one clarify the coarse and subtle according to what is known?
This point should be reflected upon. Now, the explanation is as follows:
Just as on each stage of the path of cultivation of the ten stages, there are afflictions to be abandoned,
with those of the first stage being coarse and those of the subsequent stages being subtle;
the afflictions are described as coarse or subtle in accordance with those [stages].
This case should also be understood in the same way:
within the path of seeing (darśanamārga), that which is coarse is severed first through the power of one's own discernment,
while that which is subtle is severed later through the influence of others.
There are those who, having previously suppressed the afflictions (*kleśa*), transcend to attain the second or third fruit;
however, there are none who, having previously suppressed the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), transcend to enter the second stage (*bhūmi*).
Nevertheless, once they have entered the stages, as in the case of one who gave up their body upon hearing half a verse, there are indeed those who transcend.
However, there is no transcending of great eons (*mahākalpa*),
because [the afflictions] are extremely difficult to sever;
this point should be reflected upon.
Regarding the distinct severance of each category within the nine stages of the triple realm by those of the two vehicles, there are two interpretations:
first, that they lack the capacity to transcend [the realms];
second, that within this context, they exhaustively eliminate them as well.
Since the path of the previous life also has nine grades,
and those who do not submit later likewise have nine grades, if it is granted that the path of seeing for bodhisattvas with sharp faculties is divided into three,
then the path of seeing for the two vehicles, whose faculties are dull, should also have three grades.
Why is it that there is one for them and three for these? For Bodhisattvas, the two obstacles constitute three;
for the Two Vehicles, the one obstacle constitutes two.
This is because they are distinguished as coarse and subtle.
In the sixty-ninth [topic], the "prior superior progress" (*pūrvābhyudgama*) is precisely the "subsequent preparatory application" (*paścāt-prayoga*);

The untainted [wisdom] is not like that.

Regarding this, there is one interpretation that the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which directly realizes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), is able to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Therefore, it is said in the *Sixty-fourth [Fascicle]*:
If the established truths (vyavasthāna-satya) have already been established as truths, why is it necessary to further speak of the non-established (avyavasthāna)?
Answer: Because the established truths apprehend that which possesses signs (sanimitta).
Because they possess marks, they are bound by marks and have not yet been liberated from them.
Because they are not yet liberated from the bondage of marks, they have also not yet been able to sever the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
From this, one may infer accordingly.

"Only non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) eliminates all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Regarding the second point, there is an interpretation that subsequent non-conceptual wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) eliminates those latent tendencies that are deluded regarding phenomena (*vastu*).
This is explained in the preceding text as follows:
First, it is established that the latent tendencies (anuśaya) which delude one regarding principle are abandoned, whereas those which delude one regarding phenomena are not.
Furthermore, the preceding discussion concerned the ultimate abandonment of all coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya),
and did not refer to the abandonment of the seeds of the two obstacles during the stage of a cause.
Furthermore, the preceding discussion concerned the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) regarding the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);
it was not a discussion concerning the non-established [truth] realized through subsequent cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*),
because that too is free from conceptualized characteristics (*nirvikalpa-lakṣaṇa*).
That same treatise states:
"If it were not the case that the non-established [factors] do not require conditions,
then there would be those who, possessing the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) within a mind of pure concentration, would turn toward and take the various truths as their objects."
One should abandon the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth; since those [unconditioned phenomena] are not such,
one merely excludes the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and so forth.
This does not exhaust the principle;
it is not the final word. One should consult that text for further investigation.
In the commentary, it was stated that only the two vehicles employ this [wisdom] and not the bodhisattvas;
now I shall further explain that bodhisattvas also employ this wisdom.
This is because, within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one does not exclusively abandon the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) at every moment;
rather, the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) consisting of the attachment to phenomena is also abandoned at a distinct time.
This was the explanation given by the former master regarding the mundane and supramundane paths of abandonment within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This is based on the fact that in the bodhisattva’s path of cultivation, there is a wisdom of non-conceptualization used exclusively,
which is termed the mundane and supramundane path;
there is also a wisdom that functions by unifying the ultimate and conventional truths, through which abandonment occurs.
As in the case of the superior [attainment],
although those in the lower and lowest stages do not abandon obstacles by means of the conventional [truth], they must necessarily do so simultaneously.
If it were otherwise, [the following would occur].
Is it not the case that on the subsequent superior stages, it is only non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)—
and not when conjoined with subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*)— that cuts off the afflictions? At the beginning,
it is exclusively supramundane wisdom that cuts them off, common to all three vehicles.
Since this was subsequently stated while also acting as a bodhisattva,
both principle and scripture are equal;
one may choose and reject according to one's own inclination.
The essence of the Great Nirvāṇa has two meanings.
First, the principle and the three matters are identical with True Suchness (tathatā), for within it there are the three meanings of Mahāprajñā, liberation, and the Dharma-body.
There are two entities and three matters;
because these three entities are distinct,
they are collectively termed "Great Nirvāṇa."
In the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the five untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses do not arise.
The inference (*anumāna*) is as follows:
the five tainted (*sāsrava*) sense faculties exist in the ten stages.
They certainly cannot give rise to the five untainted consciousnesses (*anāsrava-vijñāna*),
because they are comprised within the sense faculties that are tainted (*sāsrava*), non-common (*asādhāraṇa*), necessarily concomitant (*niyata-sahabhū*), and share the same object (*samaviṣaya*),
just as in the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva-avasthā*).
He speaks of permanence, bliss, self,
and purity in order to eliminate the four inverted views of the two vehicles.
This is because those of the two vehicles who have correctly realized this dharmatā [do so by means of these qualities].
It is not a conceptualization of permanence, impermanence, and so forth as being unconditioned;
rather, one enters [the state] by means of the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) forming this conceptualization of impermanence and so on.
Subsequently, when emerging from contemplation, one again contemplates what was previously observed.
Not discerning the object of focus,
one then perceives the preparatory application,
thinking that it is both the object of true knowledge and [characterized by] impermanence and so forth.
One then regards the true nature of all phenomena as being impermanent and so forth;
although these minds of preparatory application and the subsequent attainment with outflows are not of the nature of grasping, they are nonetheless virtuous.
However, because the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha) has not yet been eliminated through the six or seven [stages],
one induces a contaminated wholesome mind (*sāsrava-kuśala-citta*) to form this understanding;
thus, it occurs upon a contaminated contemplative mind (*sāsrava-vipaśyanā-citta*) that is induced by that grasping at phenomena.
It is taught that the cognitive obscurations which induce adherence to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) constitute inversion.
Since this contemplation does not arise when there is no adherence to phenomena,
it follows that from the preceding stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), one gives rise to the four inversions or the twelve inversions.
This refers to the grasping at the body and so forth as pure through perception, mind, views, and the like.
To eliminate this, the Buddha taught the practice of impermanence and so forth, describing them as being non-eternal and so on, so that they might realize [the truth].
Regarding the ultimate truth, it is neither eternal nor impermanent.
Nevertheless, because those of the two vehicles follow the Buddha’s expedient teachings and cling to their guidance,
they form conceptions such as impermanence.
Now, in order to eliminate those [misconceptions] and cause them to realize the ultimate fruit,
we teach this True Suchness as permanent and self;
this is intended to inspire such practice through skillful means so that they may enter and realize that Dharma.
At that time, it is correctly realized as neither permanent nor impermanent;
the Buddhas sometimes speak of a self,
and at other times they speak of non-self.
Within the true reality of all phenomena,
there is neither self nor non-self;
the same applies to all other categories.
This is based on Dharmapāla’s argument that only the sixth and seventh [stages] possess defiled minds characterized by grasping.
From the eighth stage onward,

Since all cases are explained according to this principle,
from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, it is no longer discussed whether the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the observing mind constitutes an obstacle.
Because within the causes of their peace and wisdom there is attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*)— whether they be untainted (*anāsrava*) or tainted (*sāsrava*)—

Furthermore, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) downward, effortful application (*prayoga*) is said to be an obstacle.
Otherwise, the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) would not be subsumed under the two types of delusion.
For this reason, all contaminated wholesome minds and their causes, being untainted, still possess attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Now, the treatise explains that true reality is neither eternal nor impermanent, and so forth.
In order to sever attachment to phenomena as being impermanent and so forth,

It reveals that its nature is free from various afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion;

The statement regarding the Dharmakāya as being "exclusively for one's own benefit" (svārtha) indicates that it is distinct from the "benefit for others" (parārtha), which is explained through a progressive series [of bodies].
As for the causes cultivated for its own enjoyment body (svasaṃbhogakāya):
It was originally cultivated for the sake of benefiting others;
furthermore, it is not mentioned because it serves as the basis for benefiting others,
whereas compared to the enjoyment of others, its meaning for one's own benefit is subtle.
For this reason, it is not mentioned;
nor does the principle exclude the enjoyment for others and the transformation bodies.
Why is self-benefit not mentioned?
Because the benefit of others by the Buddhas is itself their own benefit;
this principle should likewise hold true.
Because the mind manifests through transformation for the sake of benefiting others,
it is said to be "for the benefit of others" from the perspective of its intention (*āśaya*). This refers to the preceding stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).
It is said that all merits pertain to the two benefits [of self and others].
According to the power of one's inclination,
this [text] now follows the predominant [benefit].
Therefore, the three bodies are distinct.
Regarding the statement that the self-enjoyment body is as vast as the pure land and pervades the entire dharma-realm,
two interpretations should be made.
First, it is so in reality.
Second, it is spoken of in terms of function;
for wisdom is the Buddha.
Because that which is realized is boundless—
just as in worldly speech, one says the eye-socket is large because the place seen through it is high—
one says that wisdom is great because what is studied is vast.
Within the section on the objects of the four wisdoms,
the land of self-enjoyment consists solely of pure, untainted phenomena,
as nothing else is perceived therein.
It is known only by the Buddha.
The Land of Enjoyment for Others is fundamentally exclusively untainted and pure;
those who perceive it see only purity.
Because all the various results of maturation (*vipāka*) of unwholesome states have already ceased to exist;
yet it is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
because it is observed by the eighth consciousness and the five sensory consciousnesses as being contaminated.
As for the perceiver, they dwell in a defiled land;
their bringing of benefit and happiness to sentient beings is also manifested within defilement,
and their perception likewise extends throughout the defiled.
It penetrates the objects of all consciousnesses;
the fundamental nature of the transformed lands is exclusively untainted (anāsrava),
yet they may be either pure or defiled.
The same applies to those who see it.
It is both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), yet it may be pure or defiled,
because Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are also able to see it.
This is because the superior knows the inferior.
However, since it was originally manifested as a pure land for the sake of bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*),
the treatise states that there is a "pure" designation for this transformed land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*).
The transformed land is fundamentally for those on the stages prior to the path of seeing;
it is not specifically called "pure.
Generally speaking, when referring to the body and the land as "seen," each is designated according to its predominant characteristic.
These were spoken according to their respective levels, and thus there is no contradiction;
for those below do not know what belongs to those above.
Those prior to the stages and those of the two vehicles certainly do not perceive the untainted pure land.
All the lands herein are the objects of the four wisdoms,
appearing according to the predominant primary cause that triggers them.
It is said that wisdom manifests as distinct;
otherwise, there would be the fault of it not being universal knowledge (*sarvajñā*).
If the Buddha’s five aggregates were reckoned to be subsumed under those [same] aggregates and so forth, [it would follow that he is not omniscient].
Why is it not admitted that the Buddha is included among sentient beings?
Sentient beings depend upon maturation (vipāka),
whereas the Buddha is not a sentient being.
That which possesses the nature of being subsumed is called "dharma.
The Buddha affirmed that it is comprised within the dharmas.
The meanings of "pure" and "mixed" are explained through their differences in degree, whether superior or inferior.
This is explained solely based on the aspect of the perceived object (*nimittabhāga*). If one relies on the image (*pratibimba*), it is further said that there is a difference:
within the image, transformations belonging to one's own level (*svabhūmi*) are pure, whereas those induced by supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*) are mixed.
Within the non-supernatural powers, the eight [objects] manifest as pure conditions,
whereas the seeds are mixed conditions;
within the seventh consciousness, they are termed "pure and mixed reflections."
The reflection follows from the perception; it is said that the substance [of the object] constitutes its nature.
The five consciousnesses involve a mixture of wholesome and unwholesome minds, whereas the indeterminate mind is pure.
Regarding the sixth [category], the fivefold commonality (*pañca-sādhāraṇa*),
the application of the Dharma should be inferred accordingly.
Within the categories of the provisional and the real, there is further differentiation based on consciousness.

There are the oppositions of existence and non-existence, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the outflowing and the non-outflowing, and the objects belonging to one’s own realm and those belonging to other realms.

One should apply these principles accordingly to both pure and mixed [states]. This concludes the end of the lower volume of the *Cheng weishi lun zhangzhong shuyao* (Essential Pivot in the Palm of the Hand: A Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*).
